oneLine: A blameless man loses everything, refuses the tidy explanations of his friends, argues his case to God's face, and meets God himself, who answers not with reasons but with the vastness of creation.

author.name: Unknown Israelite poet
author.who: A highly educated writer, at home in rare Hebrew words, international wisdom traditions and the courtroom language of lawsuits. He deliberately set his story outside Israel, among 'the people of the east', so that its question belongs to every human being.
author.howWeKnow: The book names no author. Its heading simply says 'There was a man in the land of Uz' (Job 1:1), which reads like the opening of a told story. The Talmud records both a view that Moses wrote it and a view that Job 'never existed but was a parable' (Bava Batra 15a); both show that ancient readers were already unsure. Modern dates rest on language, on parallels with Mesopotamian texts about suffering, and on the book's conversation with Proverbs, Psalms and the prophets.

writtenFrom.place: Probably Judah or the Judean exile; unknown
writtenFrom.note: Nothing in the book fixes its place of writing. The non-Israelite setting (Uz, Teman, Shuah, Naamah) points to the Edom and northern Arabia region, an area known in the Bible for its wise men (Jer 49:7; Obad 1:8).

writtenTo.who: Israelites trained in wisdom, and anyone suffering without explanation
writtenTo.situation: Israel's wisdom teachers taught that the righteous flourish and the wicked fall (Prov 3:1-2). Real life, and especially the catastrophe of exile, made that look too simple. Job gives a hearing to the protest of an innocent sufferer and puts the comfortable theory itself on trial.

worldEvents.event: Mesopotamian scribes copy *Ludlul bel nemeqi* ('I will praise the lord of wisdom'), a monologue by a righteous sufferer later restored by Marduk.
The *Babylonian Theodicy*, an acrostic dialogue between a sufferer and a friend about divine justice, is composed (dating approximate).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem; the question 'why do the righteous suffer?' becomes a national question.
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon; many scholars place the final shaping of Job in the exilic or early Persian period.

backdrop:
Job is set in a world that feels older than Moses. There is no temple, no Torah, no Israel. Job offers sacrifices himself as head of his household (Job 1:5), measures wealth in flocks and servants, and lives to 140 (Job 42:16), like the patriarchs. This 'once upon a time' setting is deliberate: it lifts the story out of any one moment in Israel's history so that it can speak to all of them.

The book belongs to a wider ancient conversation. Mesopotamian texts such as *Ludlul bel nemeqi* and the *Babylonian Theodicy* also describe a pious man struck down by sickness and social ruin. What makes Job different is its shape: a prose folk tale wraps around a long poetic debate (Job 3-42:6), and the poetry refuses the happy resolution until God himself speaks. In the ancient parallels the gods restore the sufferer; in Job the deeper issue is whether a human being will love God 'for nothing' (Job 1:9).

The central debate is a clash between an honest sufferer and a theory. Job's friends hold a version of retribution theology: God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked in this life, so great suffering must mean hidden sin (Job 4:7-8; Job 8:3-6). That idea was not foolish; it is a fair summary of many proverbs and of the covenant blessings and curses (Deut 28). The problem is that they make a general truth into a rule that explains every case. Job knows he is innocent, and the reader knows it too, because God himself said so (Job 1:8).

The Hebrew of the poetry is among the hardest in the Bible, with more rare words than any other book. Translations differ widely in places, and the Greek translation is about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew. Readers should expect footnotes and should hold some verses loosely.

culture.explain: The Hebrew is *ha-satan*, 'the accuser' or 'the adversary', with the definite article, more like a job title than a personal name. He appears among the 'sons of God' (heavenly beings) presenting themselves before the LORD, like officials at a royal court, and acts as a kind of prosecutor who questions Job's motives. Later Jewish and Christian tradition identified him with the devil; the book itself keeps the focus on God's sovereignty.

Job's loss is not only pain but disgrace. He once sat at the city gate as a respected elder (Job 29:7-10); now young men mock him and spit at him (Job 30:1-10). In an honour culture, suffering looked like public evidence of God's disfavour, which is why the friends' explanation stung so badly.

The friends tear their robes, throw dust on their heads and sit with Job on the ground for seven days in silence (the length of a funeral mourning). This was right; their mistake began when they started explaining.

Job speaks like a man filing a legal case. He wants an umpire or arbiter between himself and God (Job 9:33), a witness in heaven (Job 16:19), a redeemer to stand up for him (Job 19:25), and he signs his final oath of innocence like a legal document: 'here is my signature' (Job 31:35).

God's second speech points to two great creatures. Behemoth is often linked with the hippopotamus and Leviathan with the crocodile, but both also carry the colour of ancient sea-and-chaos monsters (compare Ugaritic Lotan). God's point is that what humans cannot tame, he made and governs.

Job is not an Israelite, yet he 'fears God and turns away from evil' (Job 1:1). Like Melchizedek or Jethro, he shows that the God of Israel is known and honoured beyond Israel, and that wisdom's core is reverence for God.

jewishLens:
Jewish tradition has treated Job with both admiration and argument. The Talmud preserves a discussion of when Job lived, ranging from the time of the patriarchs to the return from exile, and the striking view of Resh Lakish that Job 'never existed but was a parable' (Bava Batra 15a); either way, the rabbis took its question seriously. Some rabbis praised Job as a God-fearer even greater than Abraham; others criticised his bitter words against heaven. Job is one of the few books that may be studied on Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the temple's destruction, because its subject is grief.

Read within Israel's covenant story, Job tests a misunderstanding of the covenant rather than the covenant itself. Deuteronomy promised blessing for faithfulness and curse for unfaithfulness (Deut 28), and many Israelites heard that as a strict formula. Job shows that the relationship with God is deeper than a contract of rewards: Job keeps addressing God, even accusingly, when God seems absent, and that persistent speaking-to-God is itself loyalty. God's verdict at the end is startling: Job, who protested, 'spoke what is right' about God, while the friends, who defended God with neat theology, did not (Job 42:7-8).

Medieval Jewish thinkers made Job a test case for providence. Saadia Gaon read it as a book about trials that refine; Maimonides (*Guide for the Perplexed* 3.22-23) read Job as moving from moral uprightness to true knowledge of God, after which his suffering no longer overwhelms him. The Aramaic Targum of Job found among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QtgJob) shows the book was studied and translated by Jews before the time of Jesus.

flow.label: Heaven tests a blameless man
flow.detail: The accuser asks whether Job serves God 'for nothing'. Job loses wealth, children and health, yet blesses God.

flow.label: Silence, then a curse on birth
flow.detail: Three friends sit with him seven days. Then Job breaks the silence by cursing the day he was born.

flow.label: Friends defend the theory
flow.detail: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar argue in three rounds that suffering means sin and urge Job to repent. Job insists on his innocence.

flow.label: Job appeals over their heads
flow.detail: Job longs for an arbiter, a heavenly witness and a living redeemer, and finally swears an oath of innocence demanding God answer.

flow.label: Where is wisdom found?
flow.detail: A poem says humans can mine silver but cannot dig up wisdom; only God knows its place. Elihu then argues that suffering can be God's discipline.

flow.label: God speaks from the storm
flow.detail: God asks Job a torrent of questions about creation, from the sea's boundaries to the wild animals, and the monsters Behemoth and Leviathan.

flow.label: Job sees and yields
flow.detail: Job says he had heard of God but now sees him, and withdraws his case.

flow.label: Friends rebuked, Job restored
flow.detail: God says the friends did not speak rightly as Job did; Job prays for them and his fortunes are restored double.

keyWords.meaning: Whole, complete, of integrity; not sinless but undivided in loyalty to God. The related word *tummah*, 'integrity', is what Job refuses to let go of.
Freely, without payment or reason. The accuser asks whether Job fears God 'for nothing'; later God says Job was ruined 'without reason'. The same word frames the whole test.
The next of kin who stands up for a family member, buys back land, frees a relative or avenges blood. Job is sure such a defender lives and will stand on the earth.
Skill in living rightly in God's world. Job 28 insists that the deepest wisdom is not a technique humans can mine but a gift tied to the fear of the Lord.
'The accuser', a title for a member of the heavenly court who challenges Job's motives.

connections.how: Proverbs teaches the general pattern that wisdom brings life; Job tests the hard cases where the pattern seems to fail. Both end at the same place: the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
Ecclesiastes shares Job's honesty about injustice under the sun and death that levels everyone.
Job's protest prayers belong to the same family as the lament psalms, which also accuse God of absence and still speak to him.
Job's patriarchal setting, long life and household sacrifices recall Abraham, another God-fearer tested by God.
James holds up Job as an example of endurance and of the Lord's compassion and mercy at the end.
Paul quotes Job's wording when praising God whom no one can put in debt.

jesusLens: Christians have heard in Job's longing for an arbiter who could 'lay his hand on us both' (Job 9:33) and a living redeemer (Job 19:25) an ache that the New Testament sees answered in Jesus, the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Tim 2:5). Jesus also embodies the innocent sufferer whom observers assume is cursed by God, and he prays a lament from the cross (Matt 27:46). Jewish readers do not read Job messianically; they see in the go'el God himself or a heavenly advocate. Both traditions agree that Job dismantles the idea that suffering always reveals the sufferer's guilt, something Jesus himself rejects (John 9:1-3).

misreadings.topic: Quoting Job's friends as God's word
misreadings.popular: Because every verse of Job is Scripture, a line such as 'whoever was innocent ever perished?' (Job 4:7) or 'God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves' (Job 11:6) can be quoted on its own as a true statement about how God works.
misreadings.inContext: The friends' speeches are inspired records of what they said, but God's final verdict is that they 'have not spoken of me what is right' (Job 42:7). Their individual sentences often sound like Proverbs; the error is applying a general pattern as a rule to Job's case. Commentators across traditions, from Carol Newsom to John Walton, read the speeches as voices in a debate that the book as a whole evaluates.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Walton and Tremper Longman agree with this. They add that many of the friends' statements are true in general (Paul even quotes Eliphaz in 1 Cor 3:19 from Job 5:13), so the issue is not that every word is false but that the friends used truth carelessly and without love.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Pastors and friends who quote the friends to sufferers repeat the very mistake God condemned. The book trains readers to ask who is speaking and how the book judges them.

misreadings.topic: Job as a story about the devil's power
misreadings.popular: Job shows that Satan causes our sickness and losses, so the key response is spiritual warfare against the enemy.
misreadings.inContext: In Job, the adversary can do nothing without God's permission and disappears from the story after chapter 2. Job never learns about the heavenly scene, and God's speeches never mention the satan. The book's focus is Job's relationship with God, not a battle with the devil.
misreadings.defence: Many evangelical teachers rightly note that Scripture elsewhere does describe a real enemy (1 Pet 5:8) and that Job 1-2 shows evil is limited by God. Both sides agree the heavenly prologue reassures readers that suffering is not outside God's rule, even when we cannot see the reason.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading Job mainly as demonology can distract from its real comfort: that one may bring raw grief and protest straight to God and still be counted faithful.

relevance.then: For Israelites who had lost land, temple and king, Job gave permission to grieve honestly, warned against glib explanations, and pointed them to a God who is free, wise and present even when silent.
relevance.now: Job teaches how to sit with sufferers before speaking, that lament is a form of faith rather than its failure, and that some suffering has no explanation we will be given. It also rebukes any prosperity message that treats health and wealth as proof of God's favour.

oneLine: Israel's songbook and prayer book: 150 poems, gathered into five books, that teach God's people to praise, complain, confess, trust and wait for his King.

author.name: David and many others
author.who: David, the shepherd-king and musician (1 Sam 16:23), heads the list, with 73 psalms headed 'of David'. Others are linked to Asaph and the sons of Korah (temple singers appointed in Chronicles), Solomon, Moses, Heman and Ethan. About fifty are anonymous. Editors and temple singers later arranged the whole collection.
author.howWeKnow: Mostly from the superscriptions, the short headings above many psalms (in Hebrew Bibles they are counted as verse 1). Some give historical settings, such as Ps 51 after David's sin with Bathsheba or Ps 3 when he fled from Absalom. The Hebrew *le-david* can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to' David, so scholars debate how much the headings claim. The New Testament cites several psalms as David's words (Acts 2:25-31; Mark 12:36).
otherWritings: 2 Sam 1:19-27 (David's lament for Saul and Jonathan)

writtenFrom.place: Jerusalem, especially the temple, and in exile
writtenFrom.note: Most psalms assume Zion and temple worship; some were written in exile (Ps 137 by the rivers of Babylon). The collection was finalised in Jerusalem in the second-temple period.

writtenTo.who: Israel at worship, gathered and alone
writtenTo.place: Jerusalem temple, homes, pilgrim roads, exile and later the synagogue
writtenTo.situation: Psalms were sung at festivals, on pilgrimage (Ps 120-134), at sacrifices of thanksgiving, in times of national disaster and in private prayer. As a finished book, the Psalter also became a guide to meditation, opened by Ps 1, which blesses the person who meditates on the LORD's instruction day and night.

setIn.note: Not a narrative, but the psalms span from the Davidic monarchy (and Ps 90, traditionally Mosaic) to the exile and return.

worldEvents.event: David makes Jerusalem his capital and brings the ark there (2 Sam 6).
Solomon's temple is built; Chronicles links temple singing to Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chr 25:1).
Babylon destroys the temple and the Davidic kingship ends, the crisis voiced in Ps 89 and Ps 137.
The second temple is dedicated; post-exilic psalms of praise and the closing Hallelujahs take shape.
The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a) at Qumran shows a differently ordered collection still in use alongside the familiar one (dating approximate).

backdrop:
The Psalms grew over about six centuries. Individual poems were written for real moments: a king going to war (Ps 20), a sick person recovering (Ps 30), the nation after defeat (Ps 44), pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem (Ps 122). Smaller collections came first, such as the psalms of Asaph (Ps 73-83), the sons of Korah (Ps 42-49; Ps 84-88) and the Songs of Ascents (Ps 120-134). A note at Ps 72:20, 'the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended', is a fossil from an earlier stage when a David collection closed there.

The finished Psalter is divided into five books, each ending with a doxology, a short burst of praise ending in 'Amen' (Ps 41:13; Ps 72:18-19; Ps 89:52; Ps 106:48), with Ps 150 as the grand finale. Many see a deliberate parallel with the five books of Moses. Gerald Wilson argued in 1985 that the arrangement tells a story: Books I-II celebrate David's kingship, Book III ends with the anguished cry of Ps 89 that God has renounced his covenant with David, and Book IV answers with Moses (Ps 90) and the cry 'The LORD reigns!' (Ps 93; Ps 96-99). Not all scholars accept so detailed a storyline, but most now read the Psalter as a shaped book, not a random hymnal.

Hermann Gunkel (early 20th century) sorted psalms by type: hymns of praise, individual and community laments, thanksgivings, royal psalms, wisdom psalms and others. Laments are the single largest group, which surprises many modern worshippers. Walter Brueggemann later described the movement of the Psalms as orientation (life makes sense), disorientation (life falls apart) and new orientation (surprised by God's rescue).

Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds; it 'rhymes' ideas. The basic unit is parallelism: a second line echoes, sharpens, contrasts or completes the first ('The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork', Ps 19:1). Learning to hear that echo is the key to reading the Psalms well.

culture.explain: Headings give author, occasion, type (*mizmor*, a song with instruments; *maskil*, perhaps a teaching poem; *miktam*, uncertain), tune names ('according to The Doe of the Dawn', Ps 22) and directions 'to the choirmaster'. The word *Selah*, used 71 times, is probably a musical or liturgical marker, meaning uncertain.

Laments complain directly to God ('How long, O LORD?'), ask for help, and usually turn to trust or a vow of praise. Complaint is permitted because the covenant binds God to his people; the psalmist holds God to his promises.
Zion, the hill of the temple, is pictured as the centre of the world, the place of God's presence and protection. Pilgrims sang going up to the feasts.

Some psalms celebrate the king, the LORD's 'anointed' (*mashiah*), at his coronation, wedding or battles. God calls him his 'son' (Ps 2:7), in the language of covenant adoption also found in 2 Sam 7:14. After the monarchy ended these psalms became prayers of hope for a coming King.

Some psalms ask God to judge enemies harshly (Ps 109; Ps 137:8-9). They are prayers of victims who hand vengeance over to God rather than take it themselves, voiced in the strong idiom of the ancient world.
Several psalms begin each line or stanza with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a way of saying 'everything from A to Z' and aiding memory. Ps 119 has 22 stanzas of 8 lines each.

jewishLens:
The Psalms have shaped Jewish prayer more than any other book. A midrash on Ps 1 says that as Moses gave Israel the five books of the Torah, David gave Israel the five books of Psalms (Midrash Tehillim 1). The Mishnah lists the psalm the Levites sang for each day of the week in the temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4), and these are still said daily in synagogue, with Ps 92 for the Sabbath. Ps 145 (*Ashrei*) is said three times a day; Ps 145-150 form the core of the morning 'verses of song' (*Pesukei de-Zimra*); Ps 95-99 and Ps 29 welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening; and Ps 113-118, the *Hallel*, are sung at Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot and Hanukkah. At the Passover meal the Hallel is split around the meal, which is likely what Jesus and his disciples sang before going to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26). Ps 126 is sung before grace after meals on Sabbaths and festivals.

Outside the liturgy, saying the whole Psalter or chosen psalms is a traditional Jewish response to illness, danger and death; communities divide the 150 among themselves so the entire book is read for someone in need.

Read covenantally, the Psalms are the relationship between God and Israel spoken aloud. They praise the LORD's *hesed*, his loyal, covenant love (Ps 136 repeats 'for his hesed endures forever' 26 times), celebrate Torah as a delight rather than a burden (Ps 19:7-11; Ps 119), and give Israel permission to argue with God on the basis of his promises. Royal psalms, especially after the exile, were read as hopes for the Messiah, the son of David; the Targum and midrash apply several of them, such as Ps 2 and Ps 72, to the King Messiah.

flow.label: Two ways and the King
flow.detail: Ps 1 blesses those who meditate on Torah; Ps 2 enthrones the LORD's anointed over rebellious nations. Together they introduce the book.

flow.label: Book I: David's cries
flow.detail: Mostly Davidic laments and trust psalms, from fleeing Absalom to quiet confidence in the Shepherd.

flow.label: Book II: longing and kingship
flow.detail: Korahite psalms of longing for God's presence, David's confession, ending with a prayer for the ideal king.

flow.label: Book III: covenant in crisis
flow.detail: Asaph wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked and the ruined temple; Ps 89 asks why God has rejected David's line.

flow.label: Book IV: the LORD reigns
flow.detail: Opening with Moses' prayer, it answers the crisis by looking past human kings to God's own kingship and the exodus story.

flow.label: Book V: return and praise
flow.detail: Thanks for gathering the exiles, the Torah meditation of Ps 119, the pilgrim songs and the renewed hope of a Davidic king.

flow.label: Final Hallelujahs
flow.detail: Five psalms of pure praise end the book; everything that has breath is called to praise the LORD.

keyWords.meaning: The Hebrew title of the book, 'praises', from the same root as *hallelu-yah*, 'praise Yah'. Even the laments are gathered under this name.
Loyal love that keeps covenant; kindness that goes beyond duty. It is the Psalter's most characteristic description of God.
Teaching or instruction, not merely 'law'. The blessed person delights in it like a tree drinking from a stream.
The king anointed with oil and adopted as God's 'son'; the source of the title Messiah (Greek *Christos*).
To wait with expectant hope, like a cord stretched taut. Waiting for the LORD is active trust, not passivity.

connections.how: Several headings tie psalms to scenes in David's life, and Ps 18 appears almost word for word as 2 Sam 22.
Chronicles describes David organising the temple singers and quotes psalm medleys at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem.
Hebrews builds its argument for Jesus' sonship and priesthood on Ps 2, Ps 8, Ps 95 and Ps 110.
Jesus quotes Ps 110 to ask how the Messiah can be David's son and Lord, and cries Ps 22:1 from the cross.
Peter's first sermon reads Ps 16 and Ps 110 as fulfilled in the resurrection and ascension.
Communal lament psalms such as Ps 74 and Ps 79 share the grief and language of Lamentations over the ruined temple.

jesusLens: The Psalms are the Old Testament book most quoted in the New Testament. Jesus said that what was written about him 'in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms' must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The early church read the royal psalms as fulfilled in Jesus the anointed Son (Ps 2:7 in Acts 13:33; Ps 110:1 in Acts 2:34-35), and saw his passion in the laments he prayed (Ps 22; Ps 31:5 in Luke 23:46; Ps 69:9 in John 2:17). Jewish readers also look to the royal psalms for the coming Messiah but do not identify him with Jesus, and they read the laments primarily as the prayers of David and of Israel. Christians have often added a second insight: Jesus not only fulfils the Psalms but prays them, so those who pray the Psalms join their voice to his.

misreadings.topic: Psalms as only 'positive' worship
misreadings.popular: Worship should be upbeat and victorious; complaint or anger toward God shows weak faith, so the lament and curse psalms are rarely sung or preached.
misreadings.inContext: About a third of the Psalms are laments, the largest single category. In the covenant relationship, bringing God your complaint is a sign of trust, not unbelief. Walter Brueggemann argued that churches which drop lament lose honesty and a sense of justice; Old Testament scholars broadly agree laments are central.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Tremper Longman, Mark Vroegop and Carl Trueman (who asked 'What do miserable Christians sing?') have also urged churches to recover lament. They add, fairly, that most laments end in trust and praise, so the goal is honest movement toward God, not complaint for its own sake.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Without lament, suffering people feel they must hide pain from God and from church. The Psalter gives them words that God himself put in Scripture.

misreadings.topic: Reading individual verses as standalone promises
misreadings.popular: Verses like 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart' (Ps 37:4) or 'no plague will come near your tent' (Ps 91:10) are personal guarantees that God will grant what I want or keep me from all harm.
misreadings.inContext: These lines are poetry within whole psalms. Ps 37 is a wisdom psalm urging patience while the wicked prosper, and the desires in view are shaped by delighting in God. Ps 91 expresses trust in God's protection; the devil himself quotes it to Jesus as a guarantee, and Jesus refuses to test God that way (Matt 4:6-7).
misreadings.defence: Careful evangelical teachers agree, while insisting the psalms do give real comfort: God does protect and does give good gifts. The point is not to empty the promises but to read them as trust in a faithful God rather than as formulas.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Formula readings set believers up for crushed faith when illness or loss comes; the psalms themselves include those very experiences.

relevance.then: For Israel, the Psalms were how a people in covenant with God talked to him: at the temple, on the road, in exile and after return. They kept alive the hope of the LORD's kingship and of a renewed Davidic king.
relevance.now: The Psalms remain the shared prayer book of synagogue and church. They teach the full range of honest prayer, give language for grief and joy, and shape worshippers to see their own lives within God's larger story.

oneLine: A parent's school of wisdom for life in God's world: short, sharp sayings on speech, work, money, family and justice, all rooted in reverence for the LORD.

author.name: Solomon, 'the wise', Hezekiah's scribes, Agur and Lemuel
author.who: Solomon, famed for 3,000 proverbs (1 Kgs 4:32), is the patron of the book. Other sections come from unnamed 'wise men', from scribes of King Hezekiah who copied Solomonic sayings around 700 BC, from Agur son of Jakeh and from the mother of King Lemuel, both probably non-Israelites.
author.howWeKnow: The book itself has internal headings (Prov 1:1; Prov 10:1; Prov 22:17; Prov 24:23; Prov 25:1; Prov 30:1; Prov 31:1). The section Prov 22:17-24:22 closely parallels the Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*, showing that Israel's sages knew and reshaped international wisdom.
otherWritings: Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (traditionally Solomonic)

writtenFrom.place: Jerusalem royal court and scribal circles
writtenFrom.note: The collections point to the royal court (sayings about kings, Prov 25:2-7) and to family teaching. Final editing probably took place in Jerusalem after the exile.

writtenTo.who: 'My son': young men being trained for adult responsibility, and through them all Israel
writtenTo.place: Households and scribal schools in Judah
writtenTo.situation: Proverbs is framed as a father and mother teaching a son as he steps into adult life: choosing friends, handling money, resisting seduction and speaking wisely. The 'son' becomes a stand-in for every reader.

worldEvents.event: The Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*, thirty chapters of advice from a scribe to his son, is probably composed in the Ramesside period (dating approximate).
Solomon's court in Jerusalem gains an international reputation for wisdom (1 Kgs 4:29-34; 1 Kgs 10:1-9).
Hezekiah's scribes copy and arrange a further collection of Solomon's proverbs (Prov 25:1).
Many scholars date the introductory chapters (Prov 1-9) and final editing to the Persian period.
Ben Sira writes in Jerusalem, continuing Proverbs' tradition and identifying Wisdom with the Torah.

backdrop:
Every ancient Near Eastern civilisation had wisdom literature. Egyptian 'instructions' were written by officials and kings for their sons; Mesopotamian scribes collected proverbs and advice. Israel's sages took part in this international conversation. The clearest example is Prov 22:17-24:22. In 1924 the Egyptologist Adolf Erman showed that many lines closely match the *Instruction of Amenemope*, and he suggested that an obscure Hebrew word in Prov 22:20 should be read *sheloshim*, 'thirty', matching Amenemope's thirty chapters (many translations now print 'thirty sayings'). Scholars still debate the direction and nature of the borrowing, but most accept a real connection.

What Israel did with this material matters more than where it came from. Proverbs grounds all wisdom in 'the fear of the LORD' (Prov 1:7; Prov 9:10), using Israel's covenant name for God. Practical skill, such as how to answer an angry person (Prov 15:1) or manage a field (Prov 24:30-34), is treated as part of living faithfully before the Creator who built the world by wisdom (Prov 3:19-20).

The book has two main types of material. Chapters 1-9 are longer speeches by a parent and by personified Wisdom, a woman calling in the streets, competing with Folly for the young man's attention. Chapters 10-29 are mostly two-line sayings, often contrasting the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, the diligent and the lazy. Chapters 30-31 bring in foreign voices and end with a poem about a 'woman of strength'.

Proverbs are not laws or promises. They are generalisations: observations about how life usually works in God's ordered world. The book itself places contradictory-seeming proverbs side by side (Prov 26:4-5) to train judgement about which one fits which situation.

culture.explain: 'Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching' (Prov 1:8). Education happened in the household. The mother's role in teaching is unusual in ancient wisdom texts and stands out in Israel's version.

Wisdom is pictured as a noble woman who builds a house, prepares a banquet and invites the simple; Folly is a loud woman who invites them to stolen water and death. The young man must choose whose house he enters.

Wisdom says she was with the LORD before creation, like a master craftsman or delighted child beside him (the Hebrew *amon* is uncertain). This poem shaped Jewish ideas of Torah as the blueprint of the world and Christian ideas of Christ as God's wisdom.
Reputation was a household's wealth. Proverbs repeatedly warns about gossip, quarrels, flattery and lies, because speech built or destroyed honour within the community.
Elders sat at the gate to judge disputes. The capable woman's husband is known there, and Wisdom calls out there; it is the public square of honour.
Proverbs is not only about personal success. It warns against moving boundary stones, bribery and oppressing the poor, whose defender is God himself.

jewishLens:
In Jewish tradition Wisdom in Proverbs became closely identified with the Torah. Ben Sira (chapter 24) and later rabbis read Prov 8 as describing Torah as God's companion at creation; *Genesis Rabbah* 1:1 opens by reading the uncertain word *amon* in Prov 8:30 as 'artisan' or 'tool', so that God looked into the Torah as an architect looks at a plan when creating the world. When the Torah scroll is returned to the ark in synagogue, the congregation sings Prov 3:17-18, 'She is a tree of life to those who grasp her ... her ways are ways of pleasantness', applying Wisdom's words to the Torah itself.

On Friday evenings many Jewish homes sing *Eshet Hayil*, 'A woman of valour' (Prov 31:10-31), in honour of the wife and mother before the Sabbath meal. Rabbinic and later Jewish readings also took the poem allegorically, of the Torah, the Sabbath or the Divine Presence, but its main life is as a family blessing.

Read within the covenant, Proverbs shows what living as God's people looks like on an ordinary Tuesday. It hardly mentions the exodus, the temple or the covenant at Sinai, yet its 'fear of the LORD' uses the covenant name and its values echo Deuteronomy: honest weights (Prov 11:1; Deut 25:13-16), care for the poor and orphans, faithfulness in marriage. Wisdom is not a self-help path apart from relationship with God; it is the fruit of trusting him with the whole of life (Prov 3:5-6).

flow.label: Purpose and foundation
flow.detail: The book exists to give wisdom to the simple and the young; its root is the fear of the LORD.

flow.label: Father's lessons and two women
flow.detail: Ten parental speeches warn against violent gangs and seduction, while Lady Wisdom and Woman Folly compete for the son.

flow.label: Solomon's sayings
flow.detail: Hundreds of two-line contrasts about the righteous and wicked, the wise and foolish, in speech, work and money.

flow.label: Words of the wise
flow.detail: Thirty sayings with close Egyptian parallels, then more sayings of the wise.

flow.label: Hezekiah's collection
flow.detail: More Solomonic proverbs with vivid images from farm, court and home, including the 'answer a fool' pair.

flow.label: Agur's humility
flow.detail: A foreign sage confesses he lacks understanding and lists numerical sayings drawn from nature.

flow.label: Lemuel and the valiant woman
flow.detail: A queen mother teaches her son to defend the poor, and an alphabetic poem praises the woman of strength who fears the LORD.

keyWords.meaning: A comparison, saying or parable; something that 'stands for' something else. The title of the book is *Mishlei*, 'proverbs of'.
Skill, whether of a craftsman, a sailor or a ruler; in Proverbs, skill in living well before God.
Reverent awe that shapes behaviour: taking God seriously as Creator and covenant Lord. It is the starting point and first principle of wisdom.
Not someone of low intelligence but someone morally closed, who will not take correction. Proverbs distinguishes the naive (*peti*), the fool and the scoffer (*lets*).
*Hayil* means strength, capability, even military valour. The same phrase describes Ruth (Ruth 3:11).

connections.how: Kings presents Solomon as the model wise king and author of thousands of proverbs, and then shows his later folly.
Job and Ecclesiastes test the edges of Proverbs' patterns; all three share the conclusion that wisdom begins with fearing God.
In the Hebrew Bible Ruth follows Proverbs; Ruth is the only person called an 'eshet hayil', a living example of Prov 31.
James is often called the New Testament's wisdom book, with Proverbs-like teaching on the tongue, humility and wisdom from above. James 4:6 quotes Prov 3:34.
Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God', drawing on the figure of Wisdom in Proverbs.
Paul quotes Prov 25:21-22 on feeding your enemy and heaping burning coals on his head.

jesusLens: Jesus taught like a sage, in short sayings and parables (the Hebrew *mashal* covers both), and claimed that 'something greater than Solomon is here' (Matt 12:42). New Testament writers drew on the figure of Wisdom with God at creation to describe Christ: 'the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24), the one 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom' (Col 2:3), the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; compare Prov 8:22-31). In the fourth century Arius used Prov 8:22 ('the LORD created me') to argue that the Son was created, which shows how influential the passage was; Nicene writers answered that it describes Wisdom's role, not the Son's origin. Jewish tradition reads the same poem of the Torah, not of a person.

misreadings.topic: Proverbs as promises and guarantees
misreadings.popular: 'Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it' (Prov 22:6) is a promise: if parents do it right, their children will stay faithful. Similarly, honouring God with wealth guarantees full barns (Prov 3:9-10).
misreadings.inContext: Proverbs are generalisations about how life usually works, not covenant promises or legal contracts. The book itself shows this by placing opposite sayings together (Prov 26:4-5) and by acknowledging that the righteous sometimes suffer and the wicked prosper (Prov 16:8; Prov 28:6). Scholars such as Tremper Longman, Michael Fox and Bruce Waltke all stress the difference between a proverb and a promise.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree almost universally on this point; it is a popular misreading rather than a scholarly debate. They add that proverbs are still reliably true as patterns: good parenting really does tend to shape children, and wise living generally leads to flourishing. The proverbs are not false when exceptions occur; they were never meant to cover every case.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Treating proverbs as guarantees burdens grieving parents with false guilt and turns faith into a formula. Reading them as wisdom frees them to guide without condemning.

misreadings.topic: Proverbs 31 as a checklist for wives
misreadings.popular: The 'woman of strength' is the standard every Christian wife must meet: rising before dawn, sewing, managing the household perfectly, never idle.
misreadings.inContext: The poem is an alphabetic acrostic, a celebration from A to Z, not a job description. In Jewish homes it is sung as praise to the wife, not as a test. Many scholars note that it also presents Lady Wisdom in household form, closing the book as Prov 1-9 opened it, and that the woman is a capable trader, landowner and teacher, not a narrow domestic figure.
misreadings.defence: Complementarian evangelical teachers often still see in her a model of godly womanhood and household leadership; egalitarian evangelicals stress her economic independence. Both agree her central quality is that she 'fears the LORD' (Prov 31:30), which applies to men and women alike.
misreadings.whyItMatters: A checklist reading can crush women with impossible standards; a praise reading invites honouring the faithful women already present.

relevance.then: Proverbs trained Israel's young people, officials and households to live as God's people in daily affairs: speaking truthfully, working faithfully, keeping marriage, protecting the poor and respecting authority, all under the fear of the LORD.
relevance.now: It remains one of the most practical books of the Bible for work, money, friendship, parenting and speech. Read as wisdom rather than formula, it builds judgement and character instead of rule-keeping or anxiety.

oneLine: A royal teacher tests every road to lasting gain, finds that life slips through our fingers like breath, and concludes that we should receive each day's food, work and love as God's gift and fear him.

author.name: Qohelet ('the Gatherer' or 'the Teacher'), presented by a frame narrator
author.who: The main speaker calls himself Qohelet, 'son of David, king in Jerusalem'. The name comes from *qahal*, 'assembly', and means something like 'one who gathers' (people or sayings). A second voice, the editor, introduces him and sums up at the end (Eccl 12:9-14).
author.howWeKnow: The book never names Solomon, but the royal experiments in Eccl 1:12-2:26 clearly wear Solomon's robes. The Hebrew is late, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah, with Aramaic influence and probably Persian loanwords; for this reason most scholars, including conservatives such as Franz Delitzsch and Tremper Longman, think 'Solomon' is a literary persona chosen by a later sage. Others, such as Walter Kaiser and Duane Garrett, have defended Solomonic authorship.

writtenFrom.note: The speaker presents himself as king in Jerusalem. A Persian or early Hellenistic date would make the writer a Jerusalem sage living under foreign rule.

writtenTo.who: Educated, reflective Israelites, and especially young people deciding what to live for
writtenTo.situation: On a later dating, Judah was a small province under Persian or Ptolemaic rule, where a commercial economy, taxes and officials created new wealth and new anxiety (Eccl 5:8-9; Eccl 5:10-12). Many asked what lasting 'profit' (*yitron*, a business word) human effort could secure.

worldEvents.event: Persia conquers Babylon; Judah becomes a province of a vast commercial empire with coinage and taxation.
Alexander the Great takes the Levant; Greek ideas begin to spread across the region.
Judah passes under the Ptolemies of Egypt, known for efficient tax-farming (dating of Ecclesiastes to this era is one common view).
Fragments of Ecclesiastes later found at Qumran (4QQoh-a) date to around 175-150 BC, setting a latest possible date for the book.

backdrop:
Ecclesiastes is the Bible's most unsettling book, and that is the point. Its key word, *hevel*, appears about 38 times. Older translations render it 'vanity', meaning 'emptiness'; the Hebrew literally means 'breath' or 'vapour', something real but fleeting and impossible to grasp. The opening cry 'hevel of hevels' (Eccl 1:2) is a superlative, like 'holy of holies': utterly fleeting, completely beyond our grip.

Qohelet describes a royal experiment. He tries wisdom, pleasure, great building projects, wealth and achievement (Eccl 2:1-11), and each time he asks what 'gain' remains. His answer is that nothing lasts 'under the sun', a phrase used about 29 times for life seen from the ground level of ordinary human experience. Death takes the wise and the fool alike (Eccl 2:14-16); injustice sits in the courts (Eccl 3:16); the righteous sometimes die young while the wicked live long (Eccl 7:15). He refuses to pretend otherwise.

Yet a second refrain runs through the book. Seven times Qohelet commends joy: eat your bread, drink your wine, enjoy life with the one you love, do your work with all your might, because these are God's gift (Eccl 2:24-26; Eccl 3:12-13; Eccl 5:18-20; Eccl 8:15; Eccl 9:7-10; Eccl 11:9-10). The answer to life's fleetingness is not despair but gratitude, receiving each day rather than trying to master it.

Scholars disagree on how the voices fit together. Some read Qohelet as a sceptic whose views the editor corrects in the epilogue. Others, like Michael Fox, see a coherent thinker honestly facing contradictions. Others, like Craig Bartholomew, read the book as a journey in which 'under the sun' observation alternates with gaps of faith ('remember your Creator', Eccl 12:1) until the editor's conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments (Eccl 12:13).

culture.explain: Life viewed from within the world of human experience, without a view from heaven. Qohelet asks what we can know and gain from observation alone.
Qohelet uses economic words: *yitron* (profit, surplus) and *heleq* (portion, share). Lasting profit is impossible, but each person does receive a portion from God to enjoy now.
Ancient Near Eastern literature includes 'royal autobiographies' in which a king boasts of his deeds. Qohelet imitates the genre and then deflates it: all his achievements are breath.
Israel's common picture of death was Sheol, a shadowy place of silence. Qohelet stresses that all go to one place and that no one knows what comes after, so we must live now.
Clean clothes, oil on the head, bread and wine were signs of festival and celebration. Qohelet commends them as fitting responses to God's gift of life.

Eccl 12:1-7 describes ageing and death with a series of images: the keepers of the house trembling (hands), the grinders ceasing (teeth), the silver cord snapped. Ancient and modern readers have decoded it in different ways.

jewishLens:
Ecclesiastes is one of the five *Megillot* (scrolls) read in the synagogue year. It is read at Sukkot, the Feast of Booths, usually on the Sabbath during the festival. The pairing is deliberate: Sukkot is called 'the season of our rejoicing', a harvest festival when Israel was commanded to rejoice (Deut 16:13-15) while living in flimsy temporary huts. A book about life's fleetingness is read in the fragile *sukkah* at the moment of fullest abundance, reminding Israel that every harvest is a gift and every shelter temporary. Some explain the reading as a check on the wealth of harvest time.

The rabbis argued about the book. The Mishnah records disagreement between the schools of Shammai and Hillel over whether Ecclesiastes 'defiles the hands', that is, counts as holy Scripture (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5; Eduyot 5:3). The Talmud reports that the sages wanted to withdraw it because its words seemed to contradict each other, but kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah (Shabbat 30b). The Midrash *Kohelet Rabbah* reads the book as Solomon's words and often finds in its 'under the sun' the contrast with Torah, which is 'above the sun'.

Read within the covenant, the book's final word ties its searching to Israel's life with God: 'fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of a person' (Eccl 12:13). Its emphasis on receiving food, drink, work and love with joy also echoes the Torah's festival commands. Qohelet is honest about death and injustice in the way Job and the laments are honest, but he keeps speaking within the frame of a God who gives, judges and is to be feared.

flow.label: All is breath
flow.detail: The motto, and a poem on endless cycles of sun, wind and rivers where nothing new happens.

flow.label: The king's experiment
flow.detail: Qohelet tests wisdom, pleasure, building and wealth; nothing yields lasting gain, but eating and working with joy is God's gift.

flow.label: A time for everything
flow.detail: God has set times for birth and death, weeping and dancing, and put eternity in human hearts without letting us see the whole.

flow.label: Injustice and toil
flow.detail: Oppression, envy, lonely labour, politics and religion done carelessly; better two than one, better listening than many words.

flow.label: Money cannot satisfy
flow.detail: Those who love money never have enough; receive your portion as God's gift.

flow.label: Wisdom's limits
flow.detail: Proverb-style advice mixed with frank admission that the righteous and wicked do not get what they deserve.

flow.label: Seize the day
flow.detail: Since death is certain and timing uncertain, eat, drink, love and work with all your strength, and take bold risks.

flow.label: Remember your Creator
flow.detail: A poem on youth, old age and death; the editor concludes: fear God and keep his commandments, for God will judge.

keyWords.meaning: Breath, mist, vapour: something real but brief and beyond our grasp. It is also the name Abel, the brother whose life was cut short (Gen 4:2).
Surplus, net gain, what is left over. Qohelet asks what lasting surplus a person gets from all their toil.
One's allotted share, like a share of land or of an inheritance. It is God's gift to enjoy now.
A long or unending time. God 'has put olam into their hearts' (Eccl 3:11): a sense of more than the present, without the ability to see it all.
From *qahal*, 'assembly'. Translated 'the Preacher' (from Greek *Ekklesiastes*, a member or speaker of the assembly).

connections.how: Qohelet's world of toil, dust and death is the world after Gen 3, and *hevel* recalls Abel, the first to die.
Ecclesiastes uses Proverbs' form but tests its confidence, admitting that wisdom cannot secure the outcomes it usually brings.
Both books challenge a tidy view of reward and punishment and end with God's sovereignty and human reverence.
Paul says creation was 'subjected to futility' in hope; the Greek word is the Septuagint's word for *hevel* in Ecclesiastes.

Paul's argument that without resurrection we might as well 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' engages the same question of death's shadow over toil; his answer is that labour in the Lord is not in vain.

jesusLens: Christian readers have often treated Ecclesiastes as the honest question to which the resurrection is God's answer. Paul says creation was subjected to 'futility' (the Septuagint's word for *hevel*) 'in hope' of liberation (Rom 8:20-21), and he ends his great resurrection chapter by saying that labour in the Lord is 'not in vain' (1 Cor 15:58), as if speaking straight to Qohelet's question about lasting gain. Jesus' teaching on not storing up treasures that moth and rust destroy (Matt 6:19-21) and his parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21) echo Ecclesiastes closely. Jewish readers, by contrast, see the book's answer in the fear of God and the commandments, and in receiving life's joys within the Torah's festivals. Both read the book as clearing away false hopes.

misreadings.topic: 'Vanity' as 'everything is meaningless'
misreadings.popular: Ecclesiastes teaches that life without God is meaningless, so the book is a negative example of a backslidden Solomon showing where unbelief leads, to be skipped until the last verses.
misreadings.inContext: *Hevel* means 'breath' or 'vapour': brief, fragile, beyond control, rather than worthless. Qohelet never says joy, work or love are worthless; he repeatedly commends them as God's gifts. Scholars such as Michael Fox ('absurd'), Craig Bartholomew and Ellen Davis show the book is a serious, faith-filled wrestling with limits, not a record of apostasy.
misreadings.defence: Some evangelical scholars, such as Tremper Longman, do read Qohelet's own voice as a sceptic's, corrected by the editor's final word. Others, like Bartholomew and Iain Provan, read Qohelet himself more positively. Both camps agree the book is inspired as a whole and that its frankness is meant to drive readers to fear God, not to be ignored.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read as 'everything is meaningless', the book seems depressing and useless. Read as 'everything is breath', it teaches contentment, gratitude and humility, and frees people from trying to control their lives.

misreadings.topic: Eccl 3:11 'eternity in their hearts' as a 'God-shaped hole'
misreadings.popular: God put eternity in the human heart, so everyone has a built-in longing for heaven that only Christ can fill.
misreadings.inContext: In context, Qohelet's point is double-edged: God has given humans a sense of the whole sweep of time, yet 'so that they cannot find out what God has done from beginning to end'. It describes both longing and frustration, the creaturely limit of knowing there is more without being able to see it.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators largely accept the context but note that the verse does point to a God-given longing, so the popular use catches something true, even if it leaves out Qohelet's emphasis on human limits.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Hearing the whole verse teaches humility about what we can understand, and trust in a God whose timing we cannot master.

relevance.then: In a commercial, foreign-ruled Judah where wealth and status were uncertain, Ecclesiastes warned against chasing control and commended a grateful, God-fearing, joyful life within limits.
relevance.now: In cultures driven by productivity, achievement and fear of death, Ecclesiastes offers sober honesty and a freeing invitation: enjoy your meals, your work and the people you love as gifts, and leave what you cannot control to God.
