oneLine: A cycle of love poems in which a woman and a man long for, praise and find each other, celebrating desire as God's good gift and love as strong as death.

author.name: Unknown poet, linked with Solomon
author.who: The title links the Song to Solomon, who appears in it as a royal figure (Song 3:7-11; Song 8:11-12). The dominant voice, however, is the woman's: she speaks more lines than anyone else, a rarity in ancient literature.
author.howWeKnow: The heading reads *asher li-shlomoh*, 'which is to/for/of Solomon'. That can mean authorship, dedication or 'in the Solomonic tradition'. The poems mention places across the land, from Lebanon and Hermon to En-gedi and Jerusalem, and include possible loanwords from Persian (*pardes*, 'orchard', Song 4:13) and perhaps Greek (*appiryon*, 'carriage', Song 3:9), which lead many to a later date; others think old love poetry was updated over time.

writtenFrom.place: Jerusalem and the land of Israel
writtenFrom.note: The 'daughters of Jerusalem' are addressed repeatedly; the imagery comes from vineyards, gardens and countryside across Israel.

writtenTo.who: Israelites at weddings and celebrations, and later the worshipping community
writtenTo.situation: Love songs were sung at weddings and feasts across the ancient Near East; Egyptian love poems of the New Kingdom period share many images (gardens, gazelles, 'sister' as a term of endearment). The Song may have been used at Israelite wedding celebrations before it was read in worship.

worldEvents.event: Egyptian New Kingdom love songs (e.g. Papyrus Harris 500, Chester Beatty I) use images close to the Song's (dating approximate).
Solomon's reign: the traditional setting of the Song and the era of its royal imagery.
Persian period: one widely held date for the Song's final language.
Rabbi Akiva defends the Song as 'holy of holies' among the Writings (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5; dating approximate).

backdrop:
The Song of Songs, meaning 'the greatest song', never mentions God directly (unless in the phrase *shalhevetyah*, 'flame of Yah', in Song 8:6, which may simply mean 'a mighty flame'). It never mentions covenant, law, temple or prayer. It is love poetry: a woman and a man describe each other's bodies with lush images, long for each other at night, search the streets, meet in gardens and vineyards, and declare that love is 'strong as death' (Song 8:6).

Scholars disagree on its structure. Some read a single story moving from courtship to wedding (Song 3:6-5:1) to married love; some read a drama with three characters, in which the woman stays faithful to her shepherd lover despite Solomon's advances; many now read it as an anthology or loose cycle of poems held together by repeated refrains. The most important refrain is the warning to the 'daughters of Jerusalem' not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (Song 2:7; Song 3:5; Song 8:4).

Its images belong to the ancient Near East. Comparing teeth to a flock of washed ewes or a nose to a tower of Lebanon (Song 4:2; Song 7:4) sounds odd in English but described beauty, strength and dignity. Gardens, fountains, spices and fruit are well-known symbols of sexual love, sometimes stated, sometimes veiled. The woman is called 'my sister, my bride', a term of tender affection also found in Egyptian love songs.

Part of the Song's power lies in what it reverses. In Gen 3:16 the woman's desire is toward her husband and he will rule over her; in the Song the woman says, 'I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me' (Song 7:10), using the same rare word for desire (*teshuqah*). Many interpreters see here love restored to the mutuality of Eden.

culture.explain: The woman is a locked garden and sealed fountain (exclusive, chaste); when she invites her beloved into her garden, the language describes the consummation of love. The setting recalls Eden.
A conventional term of affection in ancient Near Eastern love poetry, also found in Egyptian songs, expressing closeness and belonging, not literal kinship.
A poem describing the beloved's body piece by piece, from head down or feet up. The term comes from Arabic wedding songs studied in the 19th century.
In a household culture, brothers guarded a sister's honour and marriage arrangements. The woman's own 'vineyard' (her body, her choice) is a recurring image.
Song 3:6-11 pictures a royal wedding procession with Solomon carried on a litter, crowned by his mother on his wedding day.
The woman searches the city by night for her beloved; once the watchmen beat her. The scenes express the risk and longing of love in a public, honour-conscious world.

jewishLens:
The Song of Songs is read in synagogue at Passover, one of the five *Megillot*; in many communities it is read on the Sabbath of the festival, and Sephardi and other communities also recite it on Friday evenings before the Sabbath. The link with Passover comes from the long Jewish reading of the Song as the love story between God and Israel. The spring imagery ('the winter is past ... the time of singing has come', Song 2:11-12) matches the season of the exodus, and 'I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots' (Song 1:9) was read as the crossing of the sea.

The Targum to the Song turns the poem into a history of Israel, from the exodus and Sinai through the temple, exile and return, to the coming of the Messiah. Rabbi Akiva famously said that 'all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies' (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5), and the Tosefta records his warning that anyone who sings it at banquets as a secular song has no share in the world to come (Tosefta Sanhedrin 12:10). Rashi's commentary reads it as the words of Israel in exile, a wife remembering her husband's former love and longing for his return.

This allegorical tradition did not deny the plain sense of human love; it saw in human love a picture of covenant love. The prophets had already described the covenant as a marriage, with Israel as God's bride (Hos 2:16-20; Jer 2:2; Isa 62:5). Read relationally, the Song shows what covenant was meant to feel like from the inside: delight, longing, exclusive loyalty, searching and finding, and a love that 'many waters cannot quench' (Song 8:7).

flow.label: Longing and first delight
flow.detail: The woman longs for her beloved's kisses; they praise each other in the countryside.

flow.label: Spring invitation
flow.detail: He comes leaping over the hills: arise, my love, the winter is past. 'My beloved is mine and I am his.'

flow.label: Night search
flow.detail: She seeks him through the city at night, finds him and will not let him go.

flow.label: Wedding and the garden
flow.detail: Solomon's wedding procession; he praises her beauty and enters her garden.

flow.label: Absence and searching
flow.detail: She hesitates, he leaves; she searches, is wounded by watchmen, and describes him to the daughters of Jerusalem.

flow.label: Praise renewed
flow.detail: He praises her again from her feet upward; she invites him to the fields.

flow.label: Love strong as death
flow.detail: Set me as a seal on your heart; love's flame cannot be quenched or bought.

keyWords.meaning: Darling, lover; the woman's main name for the man (over 30 times). The plural *dodim* means love-making or caresses (Song 1:2).
'My darling', 'my friend', the man's name for the woman; it combines affection with companionship.
Love in its full sense; the same word used for God's covenant love for Israel (Deut 7:8).
Longing, desire; used only three times in the Hebrew Bible, linking the Song to Gen 3.
A signet or cylinder seal worn on a cord or ring, marking ownership and identity: 'set me as a seal upon your heart'.

connections.how: The Song's garden and mutual desire recall Eden before shame and reverse the distortion of Gen 3:16.
Hosea and other prophets picture the covenant as a marriage, the backdrop for allegorical readings.
Proverbs commends delight in the wife of one's youth and warns against the adulterous woman; the Song shows the delight from the inside.
Paul calls marriage a 'mystery' that refers to Christ and the church, the basis for Christian allegorical readings.
The Bible ends with the marriage of the Lamb and his bride.

jesusLens: Christian interpreters from Origen (3rd century) and Bernard of Clairvaux (12th century, 86 sermons on the Song) to Puritans such as Richard Sibbes read the Song as the love of Christ for the church or the individual soul. They drew on the New Testament's picture of Jesus as the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20; John 3:29) and of the church as his bride (Eph 5:25-32; Rev 19:7). Many modern Christian interpreters, while affirming the Song's literal subject is human love, see it pointing beyond itself: faithful human love is a living image of God's covenant love. Jewish allegory, by contrast, reads the lovers as God and Israel, and Jewish tradition does not apply it to Jesus.

misreadings.topic: A step-by-step story of Solomon's dating and marriage
misreadings.popular: The Song is a single chronological narrative of Solomon's courtship, wedding and married life, giving a model sequence and practical instructions for Christian dating and marriage.
misreadings.inContext: Most scholars think the Song is a lyric cycle, not a plot. Scenes repeat and overlap, the speakers' identities are sometimes unclear, and Solomon is ambiguous: the historical Solomon had 700 wives and 300 concubines (1 Kgs 11:3), hardly a model of exclusive love, and Song 8:11-12 may even contrast the lovers' single vineyard with Solomon's many. Scholars such as J. Cheryl Exum, Tremper Longman and Ellen Davis read the Song as poetry of love's experience.
misreadings.defence: Some evangelical teachers (e.g. Tommy Nelson, Daniel Akin) defend a narrative reading as a legitimate way to draw out the Song's progression from longing to wedding to marriage, which does appear in 3:6-5:1. Many evangelical scholars accept the Song celebrates love within marriage but caution against reading it as a manual.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Forcing a plot can turn poetry into rules. Reading it as poetry lets it shape desire, delight and faithfulness without pretending to give a dating formula.

misreadings.topic: Only allegory, or only sex
misreadings.popular: Older devotional readings treat the Song purely as a picture of Christ and my soul, embarrassed by its physical meaning; some recent readings treat it only as a celebration of sex, with no reference to God.
misreadings.inContext: Both Jewish and Christian traditions held the plain and spiritual readings together more than popular use suggests. The Song's literal subject is human love, which Scripture treats as good (Gen 2:24-25), and the prophets' marriage imagery makes a further covenant reading natural. Scholars such as Ellen Davis and Richard Davidson argue the two are not rivals.
misreadings.defence: Many traditional evangelical commentators (e.g. Iain Duguid) affirm the literal meaning while seeing the Song as a picture of God's love through the lens of the Bible's marriage theme; few defend pure allegory today.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Denying the plain sense teaches shame about the body; denying the wider sense loses the Song's place in the Bible's covenant love story.

relevance.then: The Song gave Israel a holy language for desire, beauty and faithful love, set within a covenant faith that also pictured God's love for Israel as a marriage.
relevance.now: It affirms that bodies and desire are good, that love should be mutual, patient ('do not awaken love until it pleases') and exclusive, and that faithful love is a living image of God's own unquenchable love.

sources.author: Michael V. Fox
sources.title: The Song of Songs and the Ancient Egyptian Love Songs

sources.author: Iain M. Duguid
sources.title: The Song of Songs (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries)

oneLine: The great vision of the Holy One of Israel: judgment on a faithless people, a remnant, a coming son of David, a suffering Servant, comfort and a new exodus for exiles, and a new creation where the nations come to Zion.

author.name: Isaiah son of Amoz (and, on many views, his later disciples)
author.who: A prophet in Jerusalem who had access to kings, was married to 'the prophetess' and gave his sons symbolic names (Isa 7:3; Isa 8:3). He saw the LORD enthroned in the temple in the year King Uzziah died (about 740 BC) and ministered at least until Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC.
author.howWeKnow: The heading (Isa 1:1) dates Isaiah's visions to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Narrative chapters (Isa 36-39) parallel 2 Kgs 18-20. The question is whether chapters 40-66 come from the same prophet. Isa 40-55 addresses Jews already in Babylonian exile and names Cyrus of Persia (Isa 44:28; Isa 45:1) as a figure the audience knows; most critical scholars therefore assign them to a prophet of the 540s BC, and Isa 56-66 to the restored community. Conservative scholars such as J. A. Motyer, John Oswalt and Oswald Allis defend one author, pointing to the shared title 'the Holy One of Israel' (used about a dozen times in each half of the book and only a handful of times elsewhere in the Bible), the unbroken Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, God's claim in these very chapters to announce events before they happen (Isa 41:21-23; Isa 46:9-10), and New Testament citations of both halves as Isaiah's (John 12:38-41).
otherWritings: A history of Uzziah's reign (2 Chr 26:22)
A record of Hezekiah's deeds (2 Chr 32:32)

writtenFrom.place: Jerusalem (and, on the multi-author view, Babylon and post-exilic Jerusalem)
writtenFrom.note: Isaiah of Jerusalem moved in temple and palace circles. Critical scholars place Isa 40-55 among exiles in Babylon and Isa 56-66 back in Judah after 539 BC.

writtenTo.who: Judah and Jerusalem, then the exiles, then the returning community
writtenTo.situation: Isa 1-39 addresses a nation tempted to trust Egypt or Assyria rather than God. Isa 40-55 speaks comfort to people who believed God had abandoned them in Babylon. Isa 56-66 addresses a small, struggling community in rebuilt Jerusalem, divided over who belongs and how to worship.

setIn.note: Narrative episodes run from Isaiah's call (year Uzziah died) to Sennacherib's siege and Hezekiah's illness; the oracles look ahead to exile, Cyrus (539 BC) and the new creation.

worldEvents.event: Tiglath-pileser III takes the Assyrian throne and begins aggressive westward expansion.
Syro-Ephraimite crisis: Aram and Israel attack Judah; Ahaz appeals to Assyria (Isa 7; 2 Kgs 16).
Samaria falls to Assyria; the northern kingdom ends.
Sennacherib devastates Judah and besieges Jerusalem; his annals boast he shut Hezekiah up 'like a bird in a cage' but do not claim the city's capture.
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon and soon permits exiles to return (Isa 44:28; Ezra 1:1-4).

backdrop:
Isaiah lived through the rise of the Assyrian empire, the most brutal military power the region had yet seen. In 734 BC, when Aram (Damascus) and the northern kingdom of Israel tried to force Judah into a coalition against Assyria, Isaiah met King Ahaz at a water channel and urged him to trust God: 'If you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all' (Isa 7:9). Ahaz instead sent tribute to Assyria and became its vassal. In 722 BC Samaria fell. In 701 BC Sennacherib swept through Judah, destroyed Lachish (the siege is carved on reliefs now in the British Museum) and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (Isa 36-37).

Isaiah's message is anchored in his vision of God as 'the Holy One of Israel', enthroned above the temple, whose glory fills the whole earth (Isa 6:1-3). Because God is holy, Judah's injustice, idolatry and empty worship are intolerable (Isa 1:10-17; Isa 5:1-7). Because God is faithful, a remnant will survive and a new king from the stump of Jesse will rule in justice (Isa 11:1-9). Isaiah also performed sign-acts, such as walking stripped and barefoot for three years to warn against trusting Egypt (Isa 20:2-4).

From chapter 40 the horizon changes. Jerusalem's warfare is over; Babylon, not Assyria, is the oppressor; Cyrus is coming. The prophet announces a new exodus through the desert, mocks the idols of Babylon, and introduces 'the Servant of the LORD', who is sometimes Israel (Isa 41:8; Isa 49:3) and sometimes a figure who restores Israel and suffers for others (Isa 49:5-6; Isa 52:13-53:12). The last chapters wrestle with life after return: true fasting, the inclusion of foreigners and eunuchs (Isa 56:3-8), and the promise of new heavens and a new earth (Isa 65:17).

The authorship question is real but should not obscure the book's unity of theme. Even scholars who hold to multiple authors now emphasise that the book was shaped as a single work, with key themes (Zion, the Holy One, the highway, the nations streaming to God) running from the first chapter to the last. Brevard Childs and H. G. M. Williamson have been influential in this 'whole book' approach.

culture.explain: 'Burning ones', six-winged beings around God's throne. Isaiah's vision uses temple imagery: the hem of a royal robe filling the sanctuary, smoke, and a coal from the altar to purify the prophet's lips.

Isaiah's sons carry message names: Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return', and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, 'quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil'. Immanuel, 'God with us', belongs to the same pattern of names as signs.
Isaiah sings like a wedding entertainer about a friend's vineyard that yields wild grapes, then reveals that the vineyard is Israel. Jesus reuses the image in his parable of the tenants.

Isa 44 describes a man cutting a tree, cooking his dinner over half of it and bowing to the other half as a god. In Babylon, gods were carried in great processions; Isaiah pictures them carried off as baggage on weary animals.

God calls the Persian king Cyrus 'his anointed' (*mashiah*), the only foreign ruler given this title. The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BC) records his policy of restoring displaced peoples and their gods, consistent with Ezra 1.

culture.term: The highway and the new exodus
culture.explain: Isaiah pictures a road built through the desert for God and his people to return, with water in the wilderness, echoing the first exodus.

jewishLens:
Isaiah is the prophet most often read in the synagogue. After Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the temple's destruction, come the 'seven haftarot of consolation', all from Isa 40-66, beginning with 'Comfort, comfort my people' (Isa 40:1). That Sabbath is named *Shabbat Nahamu*, 'the Sabbath of Comfort'. The Sabbath before Tisha B'Av is *Shabbat Hazon*, named after Isa 1:1, 'The vision of Isaiah', with its indictment of Jerusalem. The seraphim's cry 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory' (Isa 6:3) forms the heart of the *Kedushah* prayer recited in daily synagogue worship.

On the Servant of the LORD, the dominant medieval Jewish reading (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi) identifies the servant of Isa 52:13-53:12 with the people of Israel, whose sufferings among the nations will one day astonish the kings of the earth; this rests on texts where God names the servant as Israel (Isa 41:8; Isa 44:1-2; Isa 49:3). Earlier Jewish sources sometimes read the passage messianically: the Aramaic Targum begins 'Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper' while transferring the suffering to others, and the Talmud calls the Messiah 'the leper' with reference to Isa 53:4 (Sanhedrin 98b). Jewish tradition also preserves the story that Isaiah was martyred under King Manasseh (Yevamot 49b), which may be what Heb 11:37 refers to.

Read covenantally, Isaiah is about God's faithfulness to Zion and to the house of David despite Israel's unfaithfulness. Judgment is real, but it is the discipline of a husband and father who will not let his people go (Isa 49:14-16; Isa 54:5-8). The promised restoration is always wider than Israel alone: Zion becomes a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa 56:7), and the nations come to learn Torah from Jerusalem (Isa 2:2-4).

flow.label: Indictment and invitation
flow.detail: God sues his children for rebellion and empty worship, yet offers cleansing: though your sins are like scarlet.

flow.label: Vision and call
flow.detail: Isaiah sees the holy King, is cleansed and sent to a people who will not listen.

flow.label: Trust or alliances
flow.detail: Ahaz rejects the Immanuel sign; Isaiah promises a child-king of David's line and a shoot from Jesse.

flow.label: Nations judged, world remade
flow.detail: Oracles against the nations, then a vision of world judgment and a feast on Zion where death is swallowed up.

flow.label: Jerusalem spared
flow.detail: Hezekiah trusts God against Sennacherib and is delivered, then shows his treasures to Babylon's envoys, foreshadowing exile.

flow.label: Comfort and new exodus
flow.detail: The exile is over; God comes as shepherd, overpowers idols, raises Cyrus and leads his people home.

flow.label: The suffering Servant
flow.detail: The Servant brings justice to the nations, is rejected, wounded for others' sins, and exalted.

flow.label: New heavens, new earth
flow.detail: True fasting and justice, a Spirit-anointed herald, foreigners welcomed, and a renewed creation centred on Zion.

mindmap.center: Isaiah: the Holy One of Israel

keyWords.meaning: Set apart, utterly other, morally pure. 'The Holy One of Israel' is Isaiah's signature name for God, combining otherness with covenant closeness.
Servant, slave, minister of a king. The Servant of the LORD is Israel called to a mission, and a figure who fulfils that mission on Israel's behalf.
Comfort, console; the doubled command that opens the second half of the book.
To announce good news, like a herald running from a battlefield with news of victory: 'Your God reigns!' The Greek translation is the source of the New Testament word 'gospel'.
Those left after judgment, the seed of the future people of God.
The next-of-kin who buys back a family member. God is Israel's go'el, bound to them by family loyalty.

connections.how: Isa 36-39 largely duplicates 2 Kgs 18:13-20:19 on Sennacherib's invasion and Hezekiah's illness.
Isaiah's contemporary Micah shares the vision of nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD almost word for word.
Matthew cites Isaiah repeatedly: Immanuel, the light in Galilee, the Servant who bears our sicknesses and who will not break a bruised reed.
Jesus opens his ministry in Nazareth by reading Isa 61:1-2 and declaring it fulfilled.
Paul draws on Isaiah for the gospel to the nations, Israel's unbelief and future salvation.
Revelation's new heavens and new earth, the holy city and the end of tears draw on Isa 25 and Isa 65.

jesusLens: Isaiah has been called 'the fifth gospel'. The New Testament quotes it more than any prophet. John the Baptist is the voice crying in the wilderness (Isa 40:3; Mark 1:2-3); Jesus announces the year of the Lord's favour from Isa 61 (Luke 4:18-21) and says the Son of Man came to serve and give his life a ransom for many, language widely heard as echoing Isa 53 (Mark 10:45). Philip explains Isa 53:7-8 to the Ethiopian official as being about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35), and Peter applies 'by his wounds you have been healed' to the cross (1 Pet 2:24). Jewish interpreters read the Servant mainly as Israel or a righteous remnant and the royal oracles of a future human Messiah; they also question whether Isa 7:14 refers to a virgin conception, since the Hebrew *almah* means 'young woman'. Christians respond that the Servant both represents Israel and does for Israel what Israel could not, and that Matthew's use of Isa 7:14 follows the Greek *parthenos*.

misreadings.topic: Isa 53:5 as a guarantee of physical healing now
misreadings.popular: 'By his stripes we are healed' means healing of bodily sickness is included in the atonement exactly as forgiveness is, so believers can claim healing now by faith.
misreadings.inContext: In Isa 53 the Servant's wounds deal mainly with sin and its consequences: 'he was pierced for our transgressions'. 'Healing' is a frequent prophetic picture for restoring a sinful people (Isa 1:5-6; Isa 6:10). Matthew does apply Isa 53:4 to Jesus' healing ministry (Matt 8:16-17), while Peter applies verse 5 to forgiveness (1 Pet 2:24). Scholars such as Craig Keener and John Oswalt note both dimensions.
misreadings.defence: Pentecostal and charismatic scholars (e.g. Keener, Gordon Fee in a qualified way) agree healing flows from Christ's work and is a foretaste of the kingdom, while warning against claiming it as an automatic right. Reformed scholars such as Thomas Schreiner say physical healing is guaranteed in the resurrection, not necessarily now. Most agree the 'guarantee now' form is a popular overreach.
misreadings.whyItMatters: A guarantee reading leaves sick believers blamed for weak faith; a fuller reading holds out real hope of healing while trusting God through suffering.

misreadings.topic: Isaiah 7:14 as only a far-future prediction
misreadings.popular: Isaiah 7:14 is a straightforward prediction about Jesus' virgin birth with no meaning for King Ahaz in 734 BC.
misreadings.inContext: The sign was given to Ahaz: before the child knows right from wrong, the two kings he feared would be gone (Isa 7:16), which happened within a few years. Many scholars think a child born in Isaiah's day fulfilled the sign first, while Isa 9:6-7 and Isa 11 widen it to a royal child whose names exceed any ordinary king. Matthew then reads the whole pattern as fulfilled in Jesus. Scholars such as John Walton and Craig Blomberg defend this 'double' or typological fulfilment.
misreadings.defence: Some conservative scholars (e.g. Alec Motyer, Edward J. Young) argue Isa 7:14 is directly and only messianic, noting the unusual wording, the Greek *parthenos*, and the link with Isa 9:6. This is a genuine scholarly disagreement, not just a popular error.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Seeing the original setting shows that God's promises speak into real crises, and that New Testament 'fulfilment' often means filling full a pattern, not only matching a prediction.

relevance.then: Isaiah called Judah to trust God rather than empires, warned that holiness requires justice, and gave exiles reasons to believe God had not abandoned them and would bring them home.
relevance.now: Isaiah still calls God's people to justice for the vulnerable and honest worship, offers comfort to those who feel forgotten, and holds out the hope of a renewed creation where swords become ploughshares and every nation worships.

oneLine: A reluctant priest-prophet spends forty years telling Jerusalem that its covenant-breaking will bring Babylon, suffers rejection for it, and then promises a homecoming and a new covenant written on the heart.

author.name: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, with his scribe Baruch
author.who: A young man from a priestly family in Anathoth, a village about 5 km north-east of Jerusalem, possibly descended from Abiathar, the priest Solomon banished there (1 Kgs 2:26). Called as a youth in 627 BC, he was forbidden to marry (Jer 16:1-4), was beaten, put in stocks, imprisoned and thrown into a muddy cistern, and was finally taken to Egypt against his will.
author.howWeKnow: The book tells us Jeremiah dictated his oracles to Baruch son of Neriah, that King Jehoiakim burned the scroll column by column, and that Jeremiah dictated it again 'with many similar words added' (Jer 36:4; Jer 36:23; Jer 36:32). This is the Bible's clearest description of how a prophetic book was written. The Greek Septuagint version is about one-eighth shorter and arranged differently, and Hebrew fragments from Qumran support both forms, so the book clearly grew in stages.
otherWritings: 1-2 Kings (credited to him by the Talmud, Bava Batra 15a)

writtenFrom.note: Most oracles were delivered in Jerusalem, many in the temple courts. Jeremiah's last recorded words were spoken at Tahpanhes in the eastern Nile Delta (Jer 43:8-13; Jer 44:1).

writtenTo.who: Kings, priests, prophets and people of Judah, then the exiles in Babylon and refugees in Egypt
writtenTo.situation: Judah was caught between Egypt and Babylon. Many believed that because the temple stood in Jerusalem, God would never let the city fall. Jeremiah's message that Babylon was God's instrument sounded like treason.

setIn.note: From Jeremiah's call in Josiah's 13th year to the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon, the book's final scene (Jer 52:31-34).

worldEvents.event: The book of the law is found in the temple and Josiah's reform begins (2 Kgs 22-23).
Nineveh falls to the Babylonians and Medes; Assyria collapses.
Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish (Jer 46:2), making Babylon master of the Levant.
Babylon captures Jerusalem and deports King Jehoiachin, recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle.
Lachish letters: an officer writes that he can no longer see Azekah's signals, matching Jer 34:7 (dating approximate).
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed; Gedaliah is appointed governor and later murdered (Jer 39-41).

backdrop:
Jeremiah's forty-year ministry spans the end of the kingdom of Judah. It began under Josiah, the reforming king who purged idols after the 'book of the law' was found (622 BC). Josiah's death at Megiddo in 609 BC, fighting Pharaoh Necho, shattered hopes. His sons Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, and his grandson Jehoiachin, swung between Egypt and Babylon. Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah's scroll in his winter palace; Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah secretly but lacked the courage to obey.

Jeremiah's most dangerous message was the temple sermon (Jer 7; Jer 26). Standing at the temple gate, he told worshippers not to trust the slogan 'the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD' while they stole, murdered, committed adultery and followed other gods. He warned that the temple could become like Shiloh, the earlier sanctuary destroyed long before. He was nearly executed; elders saved him by recalling that the prophet Micah had said something similar a century earlier and had not been killed (Jer 26:16-19).

Jeremiah's confrontation with false prophets is equally sharp. Hananiah prophesied that Babylon's yoke would be broken within two years and broke the wooden yoke Jeremiah was wearing as a sign; Jeremiah replied that God would replace it with iron (Jer 28). Jeremiah urged surrender to Babylon as God's will for the time, which made him look like a traitor.

Archaeology has given the book unusual texture. Clay seal impressions (bullae) bearing the names of Gemariah son of Shaphan (Jer 36:10), Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur (Jer 38:1) have been found in Jerusalem, and the Lachish letters (about 588 BC) show the panic of the Babylonian advance. A bulla reading 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe', once linked to Baruch, is now widely suspected to be a forgery.

culture.explain: Prophets acted out their messages: Jeremiah buried a linen loincloth until it rotted, smashed a clay jar before the elders, wore an ox yoke, and bought a field while Jerusalem was under siege to show that land would one day be bought again.
Jeremiah speaks like a prosecutor bringing God's case against a faithless wife or son, calling heaven and earth as witnesses, in the style of Deuteronomy.
Jeremiah's private complaints to God, unique among the prophets, accuse God of deceiving him and curse the day of his birth, yet he cannot stop speaking: the word is like fire in his bones.
Jeremiah watches a potter reshape a spoiled pot and learns that God may change announced plans if a nation repents, or a promised blessing if it turns to evil.
A round number for a lifetime of exile, from Babylon's rise (about 605 BC) to its fall (539 BC). Daniel later prays over this prophecy and Chronicles sees it fulfilled in Cyrus.

Under the Torah a kinsman could buy back family land to keep it in the clan. Jeremiah's purchase of his cousin's field at Anathoth used sealed deeds stored in a clay jar, the same method that preserved the Dead Sea Scrolls.

jewishLens:
Jeremiah shapes the Jewish calendar of mourning. In the three weeks between the fast of 17 Tammuz and Tisha B'Av, two of the three special 'haftarot of affliction' are read from Jeremiah (Jer 1 and Jer 2), and on the morning of Tisha B'Av the prophetic reading is Jer 8:13-9:23, with its cry 'Oh that my head were waters and my eyes a fountain of tears' (Jer 9:1). Tradition calls him 'the weeping prophet' and credits him with Lamentations. On the second day of Rosh Hashanah the haftarah is from Jer 31, where Rachel weeps for her children and God answers, 'Is Ephraim my dear son? ... I will surely have mercy on him'. Many Jews still visit the traditional Tomb of Rachel near Bethlehem in connection with this text.

Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jer 29) became a charter for Jewish life in the diaspora: build houses, plant gardens, marry, and 'seek the welfare (*shalom*) of the city' where God has sent you, praying for it (Jer 29:5-7). Jewish communities have long prayed for the governments of the lands where they live, a practice rooted partly in this passage.

Read covenantally, Jeremiah is a love story gone wrong and then renewed. God remembers Israel's 'devotion' as a young bride following him in the wilderness (Jer 2:2), accuses her of running after other lovers, and grieves like a wounded husband and father (Jer 3:19-20; Jer 31:20). The judgment is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy, but it is not God's last word. The new covenant of Jer 31:31-34 is made 'with the house of Israel and the house of Judah'; its newness lies not in a new Torah but in Torah written on the heart, so that all will know the LORD and sin will be forgiven.

flow.label: Called before birth
flow.detail: God appoints a reluctant youth as prophet to the nations, to uproot and to plant.

flow.label: Faithless bride
flow.detail: God indicts Israel for leaving the fountain of living water for broken cisterns and calls her to return.

flow.label: False security exposed
flow.detail: The temple sermon: God's house is not a lucky charm for people who break his covenant.

flow.label: Prophet in anguish
flow.detail: Sign-acts, rejection and laments: Jeremiah suffers with and for his people.

flow.label: Submit to Babylon
flow.detail: Jeremiah confronts kings and false prophets, wears a yoke, and tells exiles to settle for seventy years.

flow.label: Book of Consolation
flow.detail: God promises restoration, Rachel's comfort and a new covenant written on hearts; Jeremiah buys a field in hope.

flow.label: The city falls
flow.detail: Jeremiah is imprisoned and rescued from a cistern; Jerusalem falls and survivors flee to Egypt, dragging him along.

flow.label: Nations judged, a king released
flow.detail: Oracles against Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Babylon and others; the book ends with Jehoiachin freed in Babylon, a flicker of hope.

keyWords.meaning: To turn back, return; used over 100 times in Jeremiah, both for Israel turning back to God and God turning back their captivity.
A binding relationship sealed by oath, with commitments on both sides; here broken by Israel and renewed by God.
To know by experience and relationship, not just facts. In the new covenant all will know the LORD.
Wholeness, wellbeing, prosperity. False prophets cry 'peace' when there is none; exiles are to seek Babylon's shalom.
Plans, intentions. In Jer 29:11 God's plans are for the exiled community's future after seventy years.

connections.how: Jeremiah's language of covenant, curse and circumcised hearts draws heavily on Deuteronomy, likely the book found in Josiah's reign.
Kings narrates the same final kings and the fall of Jerusalem; Jer 52 closely parallels 2 Kgs 24-25.
Lamentations mourns the fall Jeremiah predicted and is traditionally credited to him.
Daniel prays over Jeremiah's seventy years and receives a vision of seventy 'weeks' of years.
Hebrews quotes Jer 31:31-34 at length, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament.
Matthew applies Rachel weeping for her children to Herod's massacre in Bethlehem, and Jesus combines Jer 7:11 with Isa 56:7 when clearing the temple.

jesusLens: Jesus stands in Jeremiah's line. Like Jeremiah he warns that the temple has become 'a den of robbers' and predicts its destruction (Mark 11:17; Mark 13:2), weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44), and is treated as a traitor. Some people even thought Jesus was Jeremiah returned (Matt 16:14). At the Last Supper he speaks of 'the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25), and Hebrews argues that Jesus has inaugurated the new covenant of Jer 31 (Heb 8:6-13). Jewish tradition reads the new covenant as a still-future renewal with Israel, in which Torah will be fully internalised; Christian readers see it begun in Christ and the Spirit, and many add that its promise to Israel and Judah remains significant (Rom 11:26-27).

misreadings.topic: Jeremiah 29:11 as a personal promise of prosperity
misreadings.popular: 'For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a hope and a future' (NIV) is God's personal promise to me that my career, health or relationships will turn out well.
misreadings.inContext: The verse is in a letter to the whole exiled community in Babylon (the 'you' is plural in Hebrew). It follows the instruction to settle in Babylon for seventy years (Jer 29:10), so most of the first hearers would die in exile before the promise was kept. It is a promise of God's faithfulness to his people's long-term future, not a guarantee of short-term personal success. Scholars across the spectrum, including Walter Brueggemann and Christopher Wright, make this point.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Christopher Wright and Tremper Longman agree on the original meaning, but argue Christians may still draw comfort from the verse because the same faithful God has good purposes for his people in Christ (Rom 8:28), as long as 'good' includes waiting and suffering. The issue is a popular flattening, not a scholarly dispute.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read individually, the verse can collapse when life goes wrong. Read in context, it teaches patience, faithfulness in a hostile place (seeking the city's welfare) and trust in God's long purposes for a community.

misreadings.topic: 'The heart is deceitful above all things' as the whole story
misreadings.popular: Jer 17:9 proves people should never trust their feelings or desires, because the human heart is wholly corrupt.
misreadings.inContext: Jer 17:9 diagnoses Judah's stubborn idolatry, and the very next verse says God searches the heart to give each person what they deserve. Jeremiah's answer is not distrust alone but a new heart: God will write his Torah on it (Jer 24:7; Jer 31:33). The covenant story moves from diagnosis to cure.
misreadings.defence: Reformed scholars rightly see Jer 17:9 as a key text on human sinfulness, consistent with Rom 3:10-18. They agree that the promise of a new heart is essential and that believers' renewed hearts are part of the new covenant.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Quoting only the diagnosis can leave believers in permanent self-suspicion; Jeremiah holds out God's work of renewing the heart.

relevance.then: Jeremiah explained to a devastated people why judgment came, kept them from despair, and gave exiles a way to live faithfully in a foreign land while waiting for God's restoration.
relevance.now: Jeremiah warns against religious slogans that cover injustice, shows the cost of speaking truth to power, gives permission for honest complaint, and grounds hope in God's commitment to make a new covenant people.

sources.author: Walter Brueggemann
sources.title: A Commentary on Jeremiah: Exile and Homecoming

sources.author: Christopher J. H. Wright
sources.title: The Message of Jeremiah (The Bible Speaks Today)

oneLine: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction that confess sin, protest pain, and in the very middle cling to the LORD's mercies, new every morning.

author.name: Anonymous poet(s); traditionally Jeremiah
author.who: Someone who witnessed the siege and fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC: the starving children, the burned temple, the captured king. The poet speaks sometimes as a narrator, sometimes as personified Zion (a widowed woman), and sometimes as 'the man who has seen affliction' (Lam 3:1).
author.howWeKnow: The Hebrew text names no author. The Greek Septuagint adds an introduction saying Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented over Jerusalem, and 2 Chr 35:25 says Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah. Many scholars doubt Jeremiah's authorship because Lam 4:17-20 seems to put hope in Egyptian help and in King Zedekiah, both of which Jeremiah opposed; others think the tradition remains plausible.

writtenFrom.place: Judah, among the ruins of Jerusalem
writtenFrom.note: The vivid eyewitness detail suggests survivors left in the land, though some think exiles in Babylon composed or used the poems.

writtenTo.who: Survivors of the catastrophe gathering to mourn
writtenTo.place: The ruined temple site and Judah
writtenTo.situation: Jer 41:5 describes worshippers coming to the ruined temple with shaved beards and torn clothes. Zech 7:3-5 and Zech 8:19 mention fasts in the fifth month (the month of the temple's burning) observed for seventy years. Lamentations was probably used at such mourning gatherings.

worldEvents.event: Sumerian city laments such as the *Lament over Ur* had long mourned destroyed cities and departed gods, a genre Lamentations shares and transforms.
Nebuchadnezzar's army begins the final siege of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 25:1).
The wall is breached, Zedekiah captured and blinded, and the temple burned (2 Kgs 25:4-9).
A further deportation from Judah follows the murder of Gedaliah (Jer 52:30).

backdrop:
In 586 BC, after an eighteen-month siege, Babylon broke into Jerusalem. Famine had been so severe that mothers ate their children (Lam 2:20; Lam 4:10), a horror Deuteronomy had named among the covenant curses (Deut 28:53-57). Nebuchadnezzar's commander burned the temple, the palace and the great houses, pulled down the walls and deported much of the population (2 Kgs 25:8-11). For Judah, it was not only a military defeat; it seemed the end of the covenant promises of land, king and temple.

Lamentations gives words to that grief. Its five poems are carefully built. Chapters 1, 2 and 4 are alphabetic acrostics of 22 verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 is a triple acrostic: three verses for each letter, 66 in all. Chapter 5 has 22 verses but is not an acrostic, as if the poet's control finally breaks down into raw prayer. The acrostic form may express completeness, grief 'from A to Z', or impose order on chaos. Many lines use a limping rhythm, called *qinah* (lament) metre, with a long line followed by a shorter one, like a sob.

The book holds two things together without resolving them. It confesses that the disaster was the LORD's just judgment for Jerusalem's sin (Lam 1:8; Lam 1:18). It also protests that the suffering is excessive and asks God to look at what he has done (Lam 2:20; Lam 5:20). In the exact centre of the book stands the confession that the LORD's steadfast love never ceases and his mercies are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23). Yet the book ends not with resolution but with a question: 'unless you have utterly rejected us' (Lam 5:22).

culture.explain: Jerusalem is personified as a woman who has lost husband and children, sitting alone with 'none to comfort her', a phrase repeated five times in chapter 1.
Sitting on the ground in silence, throwing dust on the head, wearing sackcloth, shaving beards: the gestures of a funeral applied to a whole city.

Each verse or group of verses starts with the next Hebrew letter. In chapters 2-4 the letters *pe* and *ayin* appear in reverse of the usual order, an alphabet order also known from some ancient inscriptions.
Many images (famine, cannibalism, exile, enemies mocking) match the curses of Deut 28 and Lev 26 almost point by point.
Shockingly, the poet describes God himself as acting like an enemy, bending his bow and tearing down his own sanctuary.
'The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed' refers to King Zedekiah, captured as he fled, showing how much hope rested on the Davidic king.

jewishLens:
Lamentations, called *Eikhah* ('How!') from its first word, is chanted in synagogues on the evening of Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, the fast day that mourns the destruction of both the first temple (586 BC) and the second (AD 70) and later disasters of Jewish history. Worshippers sit on the floor or on low stools, as mourners do, often by dim light, while the book is sung to a haunting melody used for nothing else. When the reader reaches the end, the congregation repeats the second-last verse, 'Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored; renew our days as of old' (Lam 5:21), so the book does not close on the bleak final line. The same custom is followed with Isaiah, Malachi and Ecclesiastes. Other prophetic readings in the weeks around the fast link the 'eikhah' cries of Moses (Deut 1:12), Isaiah (Isa 1:21) and Jeremiah.

The midrash *Eikhah Rabbah* is one of the oldest rabbinic commentaries. It pictures God himself mourning over the destruction, like a king who has lost his sons, and even weeping; the rabbis did not shrink from describing God as sharing his people's grief. Medieval *kinot* (elegies) recited on Tisha B'Av extend Lamentations to new tragedies, from the Crusades to the Holocaust.

Covenantally, Lamentations is the darkest page of the relationship between God and Israel: the curses of Deuteronomy have fallen. Yet the poets still speak to God, still call him 'LORD', still remember his hesed and still ask him to remember them. Faith here is not explaining the disaster but refusing to stop addressing the covenant partner who allowed it.

flow.label: The lonely widow
flow.detail: Jerusalem sits desolate, betrayed by her lovers, and herself cries out: is it nothing to you, all who pass by?

flow.label: God's anger described
flow.detail: The Lord has swallowed up his own city and temple as an enemy; children faint in the streets.

flow.label: One man's affliction
flow.detail: A sufferer describes God as a bear in ambush and an archer, until he remembers.

flow.label: Mercies new every morning
flow.detail: At the book's centre: the LORD's steadfast love never ceases; it is good to wait quietly.

flow.label: Examine and return
flow.detail: Let us test our ways and lift our hearts to God; the sufferer pleads for justice.

flow.label: Horrors of the siege
flow.detail: Gold grows dim; princes starve; the anointed king is captured; Edom will be judged.

flow.label: Remember us
flow.detail: A communal prayer listing the people's disgrace, ending with 'restore us' and an unanswered question.

keyWords.meaning: A cry of shock and grief, 'How can this be?'; the book's Hebrew title.
Covenant loyalty and kindness; the plural 'steadfast loves' (*hasdei*) in Lam 3:22 suggests many acts of kindness.
Tender compassion, related to *rehem*, 'womb': the feeling of a mother for her child.
Steadiness, reliability, trustworthiness. 'Great is your faithfulness' is spoken in the middle of the ruins.
One who consoles. Zion has none; Isaiah later answers 'Comfort, comfort my people'.

connections.how: Jeremiah predicted the catastrophe Lamentations mourns, and shares its tears and imagery.
Lamentations describes the covenant curses of Deut 28 fulfilled, including the siege famine.
Isa 40-55 answers Lamentations' 'no one to comfort her' with 'Comfort, comfort my people', and pictures Zion's children returning.
Communal laments over the destroyed temple share the same grief and questions.
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foresees its destruction in language recalling the first fall.

jesusLens: Christians have long read Lam 1:12, 'Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow', in Holy Week as words fitting Christ on the cross; the man 'who has seen affliction' of Lam 3 has also been read as a figure of the suffering Christ, and parts of Lamentations are sung in the Tenebrae services of the Catholic and Anglican traditions. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and predicted a second destruction (Luke 19:41-44), which came in AD 70 and is also mourned on Tisha B'Av. Jewish tradition reads the book as the mourning of Israel and of God himself, not as messianic prophecy. Both traditions find in Lam 3:22-33 the conviction that God 'does not willingly afflict' and that his compassion outlasts judgment.

misreadings.topic: 'Great is thy faithfulness' lifted out of the ruins
misreadings.popular: Lam 3:22-23 is a cheerful promise of fresh blessings each day, sung as an upbeat hymn without reference to its setting.
misreadings.inContext: The verses are spoken in the middle of a devastated city, by a man who has just described God as an enemy who broke his bones. They are a defiant act of memory ('this I call to mind', Lam 3:21), not a summary of how things feel. Scholars such as Kathleen O'Connor and F. W. Dobbs-Allsopp stress that the book's hope is fragile and surrounded by unresolved grief.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars and hymn-singers would agree; the hymn by Thomas Chisholm (1923) itself was written by a man of modest means and ill health and celebrates God's faithfulness through hardship. The point is not to stop singing it but to sing it as Lamentations does, in honesty about pain.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read in context, the verse gives hope to people whose lives are in ruins, not just to those having a good day; it also legitimises grief alongside faith.

misreadings.topic: Confession means no complaint
misreadings.popular: Because the disaster was God's just judgment, the right response is only to accept it quietly; questioning God would be rebellion.
misreadings.inContext: Lamentations does both. It confesses sin (Lam 1:18; Lam 3:42) but also asks God to see whether anyone was ever treated like this (Lam 2:20) and ends with an unresolved plea (Lam 5:20-22). Adele Berlin and Dobbs-Allsopp note that protest and confession sit side by side within covenant faith.
misreadings.defence: Traditional evangelical commentators such as Tremper Longman note that Lam 3:39 warns against complaining about the punishment of sin, so there is a real tension; but they also accept that the book's protests are inspired prayers. The book holds both without cancelling either.
misreadings.whyItMatters: This balance helps people who suffer because of their own sin, and those who suffer far beyond it, to speak honestly to God.

relevance.then: Lamentations gave survivors of the greatest catastrophe of Israel's history a structured way to grieve, confess and pray together, keeping them in relationship with God when everything else was gone.
relevance.now: It models communal grief after disasters, wars and abuses; shows that faith can hold confession, protest and hope at the same time; and gives words to anyone who has seen their world collapse.

sources.author: Kathleen M. O'Connor
sources.title: Lamentations and the Tears of the World

oneLine: A priest in exile sees God's glory on a moving throne, watches it leave the defiled temple, and then sees it return to a renewed people, raised from death and given a new heart and spirit.

author.name: Ezekiel son of Buzi
author.who: A priest from Jerusalem, trained for temple service, deported to Babylonia with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. He lived in his own house at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal, where the elders of the exiles came to consult him (Ezek 3:15; Ezek 8:1). His wife, 'the delight of his eyes', died suddenly, and he was told not to mourn publicly as a sign (Ezek 24:15-24).
author.howWeKnow: The book is mostly in the first person and is dated more precisely than any other prophetic book, with about thirteen dates counted from Jehoiachin's exile (e.g. Ezek 1:2; Ezek 8:1; Ezek 33:21; Ezek 40:1). Its priestly vocabulary closely resembles the Holiness Code of Lev 17-26. Most scholars accept that the core comes from Ezekiel, arranged and expanded by his disciples.

writtenFrom.place: Tel-abib by the Chebar canal, Babylonia
writtenFrom.note: The Chebar (*nar kabari*) was an irrigation canal near Nippur, known from Babylonian business documents of the Murashu family. The exact location of Tel-abib is unknown; coordinates are approximate for the Nippur region.

writtenTo.who: Judean exiles of the first deportation, and through them the whole house of Israel
writtenTo.situation: Before 586 BC the exiles expected a quick return and believed Jerusalem could never fall. After it fell they swung to despair: 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost' (Ezek 37:11). Ezekiel had to destroy false hope first, then build true hope.

setIn.note: From Ezekiel's inaugural vision in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile to his last dated oracle in the twenty-seventh year (Ezek 29:17).

worldEvents.event: Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem and deports Jehoiachin, Ezekiel and leading citizens (2 Kgs 24:10-16).
Babylonian ration tablets from this era list 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahud' and his sons receiving oil in Babylon (dating approximate).
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed; a refugee brings the news to Ezekiel (Ezek 33:21).
Nebuchadnezzar begins a thirteen-year siege of Tyre, reflected in Ezek 26-29 (dating approximate).
Nebuchadnezzar dies; Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) releases Jehoiachin (2 Kgs 25:27).

backdrop:
Ezekiel was thirty, the age priests began serving (Num 4:3), when he received his call (Ezek 1:1 likely refers to his age). But there was no temple in Babylon. Instead, God came to him: a storm from the north, four living creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, and above them a sapphire throne with 'the likeness of the glory of the LORD' (Ezek 1:26-28). The point is that God's presence is not trapped in Jerusalem; his throne is mobile and can reach exiles by a Babylonian canal.

The first half of the book (Ezek 1-24) explains why Jerusalem must fall. Ezekiel acts out the siege with a clay brick, lies on his side for months, eats rationed bread cooked over dung, and shaves his head and divides the hair (Ezek 4-5). In a vision he is carried to the temple and sees idol worship, women weeping for the god Tammuz, and men bowing to the sun (Ezek 8). Then the glory of the LORD leaves the temple in stages and halts on the Mount of Olives (Ezek 10:18-19; Ezek 11:22-23). For a priest, this was the most terrible sight imaginable.

After oracles against seven nations (Ezek 25-32), the turning point comes when a refugee announces, 'The city has fallen' (Ezek 33:21). From then on Ezekiel speaks hope: a true shepherd from David's line (Ezek 34), a new heart and spirit (Ezek 36), dry bones raised to life and two kingdoms reunited (Ezek 37), the defeat of Gog (Ezek 38-39), and a vast, measured temple to which the glory returns, with a river flowing from it to heal the Dead Sea (Ezek 40-48). The final name of the city is 'The LORD is there' (Ezek 48:35).

Ezekiel is the strangest of the prophets: his visions are overwhelming, his allegories (Ezek 16; Ezek 23) are sexually graphic, and his behaviour was so unusual that some modern writers have tried to diagnose him. Most scholars now read his actions as deliberate prophetic theatre, and his graphic language as a shock tactic to make complacent hearers feel the outrage of covenant betrayal.

culture.explain: The visible, radiant presence of God that filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. Its departure and return frame the whole book.

Composite throne guardians with faces of a human, lion, ox and eagle. Similar winged guardians (lamassu) stood at Assyrian and Babylonian palace gates, but in Ezekiel they carry the throne of Israel's God.
Ezekiel's dramatic actions, such as the brick siege model, lying on his side, digging through a wall with baggage, and not mourning his wife, made the message visible to a sceptical audience.
A city watchman who failed to warn of attack bore responsibility for the deaths. Ezekiel is made a watchman for Israel, accountable for sounding the warning.

Ancient Near Eastern kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel indicts Israel's rulers as shepherds who fed themselves, and promises that God himself, through a Davidic prince, will shepherd the flock.
As a priest Ezekiel thinks in terms of clean and unclean, holy and common. Idolatry and bloodshed defile the land so that God's holy presence cannot remain; the new temple restores clear boundaries.

jewishLens:
Ezekiel's opening vision became the foundation of Jewish mystical tradition, called *ma'aseh merkavah*, 'the work of the chariot'. The Mishnah restricts teaching it: the chariot may not be expounded even to one student unless he is a sage who understands on his own (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1). Yet Ezek 1 is read publicly as the haftarah on the first day of Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah, pairing the revelation at Sinai with the revelation to Ezekiel. Ezek 37, the valley of dry bones, is the haftarah for the Sabbath during Passover, linking the exodus with national resurrection; it became an important text for the Jewish belief in the resurrection of the dead, and after the Holocaust it was often read as a picture of the Jewish people's survival.

The rabbis also wrestled with Ezekiel. Because his temple regulations (Ezek 40-48) differ in places from the laws of the Torah, the Talmud reports that the sages considered withdrawing the book until Hananiah ben Hezekiah sat in an upper room with three hundred jars of oil for his lamp and worked out how to reconcile them (Shabbat 13b). Many details are left for Elijah to explain when he comes.

Covenantally, Ezekiel insists that God acts 'for the sake of my holy name' (Ezek 36:22): his reputation is bound up with Israel's fate among the nations, so he will restore them, not because they earned it but because he is faithful. The refrain 'then they will know that I am the LORD', about 70 times, shows that the goal of judgment and restoration is relationship: 'you shall be my people, and I will be your God' (Ezek 36:28). The new heart and new spirit of Ezek 36 parallel Jeremiah's new covenant, with Torah obeyed from within.

flow.label: Vision of the mobile throne
flow.detail: By a Babylonian canal, Ezekiel sees God's glory on a living, wheeled throne and is commissioned as a watchman.

flow.label: Siege acted out
flow.detail: Brick model, lying on his side, rationed bread and shaved hair announce Jerusalem's coming siege.

flow.label: The glory departs
flow.detail: Ezekiel sees idolatry in the temple; the glory moves to the threshold, the east gate and then the mountain east of the city.

flow.label: Allegories and responsibility
flow.detail: Jerusalem as an unfaithful foundling-bride; each generation answers for its own sin; God takes no pleasure in death.

flow.label: Nations judged
flow.detail: Oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon and Egypt, including the proud king of Tyre.

flow.label: The city has fallen
flow.detail: News arrives; Ezekiel's mouth is opened, and his message turns to hope.

flow.label: Shepherd, new heart, dry bones
flow.detail: God will shepherd his flock, give a new heart and spirit, raise the nation from death and unite it under one king.

flow.label: The glory returns
flow.detail: After Gog's defeat, a vision of a new temple, the glory's return, a life-giving river and a city named 'The LORD is there'.

mindmap.center: Ezekiel: the glory leaves and returns

keyWords.meaning: Weight, heaviness, honour; the radiant manifest presence of God.
'Human being', 'mortal'; God's address to Ezekiel about 93 times, stressing his frailty before the divine glory.
One Hebrew word for wind, breath and spirit. In the valley of bones the play on all three meanings is deliberate.
'You will know that I am the LORD': the goal of all God's acts, an experiential, relational knowing.
Shepherd, ruler, pastor. God promises to shepherd his people himself and through his servant David.

connections.how: Ezekiel's priestly language of holiness, defilement and covenant blessing and curse closely mirrors Lev 17-26.
Jeremiah and Ezekiel both promise a renewed heart and covenant, and both quote and reject the proverb about sour grapes.
Jesus presents himself as the good shepherd and promises rivers of living water and new birth by water and Spirit, all strongly echoing Ezekiel.
Revelation reuses Ezekiel's throne vision, eating the scroll, Gog and Magog, the measured temple and the river of life.
Ezekiel names a righteous 'Daniel' alongside Noah and Job; Daniel's vision of one like a son of man on clouds develops throne-vision imagery.

jesusLens: Christians read Ezekiel's promises as fulfilled in Jesus and the Spirit. Jesus is the shepherd who seeks the lost (Luke 15:3-7; John 10:11), the Davidic king Ezekiel promised (Ezek 34:23-24). His body is the temple where God's glory dwells (John 1:14; John 2:19-21), and from him and the Spirit flow 'rivers of living water' like the river from Ezekiel's temple (John 7:37-39). The new heart and spirit of Ezek 36 lie behind Jesus' words about being born of water and Spirit (John 3:5) and the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost. Revelation ends with a city where God dwells with his people, echoing 'The LORD is there' (Rev 21:3; Rev 22:1-2). Jewish readers expect Ezekiel's restoration literally: a regathered Israel, a Davidic king and a third temple, and read the dry bones as national and bodily resurrection.

misreadings.topic: Gog of Magog as a coded prediction about Russia
misreadings.popular: Ezek 38-39 predicts that in the end times Russia ('Rosh', with 'Meshech' as Moscow and 'Tubal' as Tobolsk) will lead a coalition including Iran (Persia) against modern Israel, and current events show this is about to happen.
misreadings.inContext: Most scholars, conservative and critical, identify Meshech and Tubal with peoples of Anatolia (modern Turkey) known from Assyrian records (Mushku and Tabal). The Hebrew *rosh* most naturally means 'chief' ('Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'), not a nation. Gog is a symbolic final enemy drawn from the far north, the edge of the known world, whose defeat shows that restored Israel will be secure because God protects it. Scholars such as Daniel Block and Iain Duguid make these points.
misreadings.defence: Dispensational writers such as John Walvoord and Mark Hitchcock defend a future literal invasion and some still argue for 'Rosh' as a people; but many dispensational scholars now concede the Russia identification is weak. A future, literal fulfilment in some form remains a legitimate view, debated against symbolic and already-fulfilled readings.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Matching Ezekiel to the news has produced repeated failed predictions and can turn prophecy into speculation. Read in context, Gog's defeat assures God's people that no enemy can undo his restoration.

misreadings.topic: Ezekiel 28 as the story of Satan's fall
misreadings.popular: The lament over the king of Tyre, 'You were in Eden, the garden of God ... you were an anointed guardian cherub', describes Lucifer's original glory and fall before creation.
misreadings.inContext: The oracle is explicitly addressed to 'the king of Tyre', whose pride came from trade and wealth (Ezek 28:5; Ezek 28:16). Ezekiel uses Eden imagery and perhaps ancient myths of a primeval figure on God's mountain to mock a human king who thought himself a god (Ezek 28:2). Most commentators, including Block and Greenberg, read it as a taunt against the king, not a hidden history of Satan.
misreadings.defence: A line of interpreters from Tertullian and Origen to some modern evangelicals sees a double reference: the human king as an instance of a deeper spiritual pride whose origin is in Satan. Scholars who hold this usually grant that the passage's primary target is the king of Tyre. It is a real debate, not just a popular error.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading the text first as a warning about human pride and economic power keeps its point sharp for today; any further application must not erase that.

relevance.then: Ezekiel shattered false hope in an unbreakable Jerusalem, explained the disaster as the holy God's just response, and then gave exiles who felt dead a vision of resurrection, renewal and God's presence among them again.
relevance.now: Ezekiel warns leaders who exploit those in their care, insists on personal responsibility, and offers hope that God can give new hearts and breathe life into what seems dead, for individuals and communities.

oneLine: Stories of Jewish exiles who stay faithful at a pagan court, and visions of beastly empires, all declaring that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and will give the everlasting kingdom to 'one like a son of man' and his holy people.

author.name: Daniel (traditional); an anonymous author or circle in the Maccabean era (critical view)
author.who: Daniel, whose Babylonian name was Belteshazzar, was a young Judean noble taken to Babylon, trained in Babylonian learning and serving as an adviser to kings for about seventy years. On the critical view, the book's final author was a wise teacher among the *maskilim*, 'those who are wise' (Dan 11:33; Dan 12:3), during the persecution of 167-164 BC.
author.howWeKnow: The visions (Dan 7-12) are written in the first person by Daniel. The traditional date rests on these claims, on Jesus' reference to 'the prophet Daniel' (Matt 24:15), on accurate details such as Belshazzar's role as co-regent (once doubted, now confirmed by the Nabonidus texts), and on Daniel's presence at Qumran by about 125-100 BC. The critical date rests on the detail of Dan 11, which tracks events from Alexander through the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings with growing precision up to Antiochus IV's desecration of the temple in 167 BC, and then, many argue, gets the details of Antiochus' death wrong (Dan 11:40-45). Other arguments include Greek loanwords for musical instruments (Dan 3:5), puzzles over 'Darius the Mede' (unknown outside the Bible) and the book's place among the Writings rather than the Prophets. Conservative scholars such as Joyce Baldwin, Ernest Lucas (who leans to a mixed view), Stephen Miller and Tremper Longman have responses to each.

writtenFrom.note: The stories are set in Babylon and Susa (Dan 8:2). If the final book is Maccabean, it was likely completed in Judea.

writtenTo.who: Jews living under foreign empires, especially those facing pressure to give up their faith
writtenTo.place: The exile, the Persian diaspora, and Judea under Antiochus IV
writtenTo.situation: Whether read as sixth-century exiles or second-century martyrs, the audience faced the same question: how to be faithful to God when pagan powers demand total loyalty. Under Antiochus IV (167 BC) Sabbath, circumcision and Torah scrolls were banned and an altar to Zeus was set up in the temple, the 'abomination that makes desolate' (Dan 11:31).

setIn.note: From Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation in the third year of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1) to Daniel's last vision in the third year of Cyrus (Dan 10:1).

worldEvents.event: Nebuchadnezzar becomes king of Babylon and takes the first Judean captives.
Persia captures Babylon; the Nabonidus Chronicle describes the city's fall, while Nabonidus' son Belshazzar was in charge of Babylon.
Alexander the Great defeats Persia, the 'goat' of Dan 8 that breaks the ram's two horns.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes desecrates the temple and bans Jewish practice, sparking the Maccabean revolt.
Judas Maccabeus rededicates the temple, the origin of Hanukkah; Antiochus dies in Persia.

backdrop:
Daniel is two books in one. Chapters 1-6 are court tales, stories about Jews at a foreign king's court, like the Joseph story (Gen 41) and Esther. Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food, interpret dreams, survive a blazing furnace and a lions' den, and see proud kings humbled. Chapters 7-12 are apocalyptic visions: four beasts from the sea, a ram and a goat, seventy 'weeks' of years, and a long revelation about the 'kings of the north and south'. 'Apocalyptic' comes from the Greek for 'unveiling'; it uses symbols, angels and numbers to reveal what is happening behind history and how it will end.

The book is also bilingual. It begins in Hebrew, switches to Aramaic, the international language of the empires, from the moment the Babylonian wise men speak to the king (Dan 2:4) to the end of chapter 7, then returns to Hebrew. The Aramaic section has a careful mirror structure: four kingdoms (Dan 2 and Dan 7), faithful Jews delivered (Dan 3 and Dan 6), and proud kings judged (Dan 4 and Dan 5).

The date of Daniel is one of the sharpest disagreements in Old Testament studies. Most critical scholars hold that the visions were written between 167 and 164 BC to strengthen Jews under Antiochus IV, using older stories from the Persian or early Greek period; this was first argued by the pagan philosopher Porphyry and is now standard in mainstream scholarship (John Collins, Carol Newsom). Conservative scholars hold a sixth-century date, accepting predictive prophecy and pointing to the book's accurate Babylonian details. Some evangelical scholars (for example, John Goldingay) accept a second-century date while affirming the book's inspiration, arguing that the visions may be written as prophecy in the style of their genre.

The four kingdoms of Dan 2 and Dan 7 illustrate the debate. The traditional reading, found already in Josephus and Jerome, is Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, with God's kingdom arriving in the Roman era. The critical reading is Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, with the 'little horn' as Antiochus IV and the kingdom expected in his time. Either way, the book's message is that God gives kingdoms to whom he wills and will replace all of them with his own (Dan 2:44; Dan 4:17).

culture.explain: Eating the king's food bound a courtier to the king as a client to his patron, and the meat may not have been kosher or may have been offered to idols. Daniel's request for vegetables and water kept a mark of loyalty to God while serving faithfully.
Babylonian names honoured Babylonian gods: Belteshazzar ('protect the king's life', perhaps invoking Bel), Abednego ('servant of Nabu'). Renaming marked a change of owner and identity.
Babylonian scholars kept huge dream-omen manuals. Daniel, like Joseph, can do what professional experts cannot because God reveals mysteries.
Daniel prays three times a day facing Jerusalem, following Solomon's prayer that exiles would pray toward the land and the temple.
Beasts stand for empires, horns for kings, the sea for chaos, clouds for divine presence, and numbers (seven, seventy, 'time, times and half a time') for periods set by God.
Daniel introduces named angels: Gabriel, who explains visions, and Michael, 'the great prince' who protects Israel. Nations have heavenly 'princes' too, an idea linked to Deut 32:8.

jewishLens:
In the Hebrew Bible Daniel is placed among the Writings (*Ketuvim*), not the Prophets. The Talmud reflects this, distinguishing Daniel from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Megillah 3a). Some explain the placement by the book's late date, others by its genre, or by the view that Daniel was a wise man to whom God revealed things rather than a prophet sent to Israel. Daniel is not read as a haftarah in the synagogue, but its heroes are honoured as models of *kiddush ha-Shem*, sanctifying God's name by being ready to die rather than worship idols. Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah (Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego) are remembered in the Talmud and liturgy alongside other martyrs.

The book is closely tied to Hanukkah. The persecution under Antiochus IV and the 'abomination of desolation' (Dan 11:31; Dan 12:11) are the events from which the Maccabees rescued the temple. 1 Maccabees uses Daniel's language of 'the desolating sacrilege', and Mattathias' farewell speech cites Daniel and his friends as models (according to 1 Macc 2:59-60).

Rabbinic interpreters often read Daniel's visions messianically, but carefully. The Talmud warns against calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b), even as some sages explored Daniel's numbers. Rashi read the seventy weeks of Dan 9 as ending with the Roman destruction of the second temple in AD 70. The 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds (Dan 7:13) was read both as the Messiah (Sanhedrin 98a contrasts his coming 'with the clouds' and 'lowly, riding on a donkey', Zech 9:9) and, as Dan 7:18 and Dan 7:27 suggest, as a symbol of 'the holy ones of the Most High', faithful Israel. Covenantally, Daniel's prayer in chapter 9 is a model: he confesses Israel's sin, appeals to God's covenant faithfulness and to his name, and asks God to act 'for your own sake' (Dan 9:4-19).

flow.label: Faithful at the king's table
flow.detail: Four young exiles refuse the king's food and are blessed with wisdom.

flow.label: Statue of four kingdoms
flow.detail: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a statue smashed by a stone that becomes a mountain: God's everlasting kingdom.

flow.label: Furnace and humbled king
flow.detail: Three friends refuse to bow and are rescued in the fire; Nebuchadnezzar goes mad until he acknowledges the Most High.

flow.label: Writing on the wall and lions
flow.detail: Belshazzar profanes temple vessels and loses his kingdom that night; Daniel prays despite a decree and is saved from the lions.

flow.label: Beasts and the son of man
flow.detail: Four beasts rise from the sea; the Ancient of Days gives everlasting dominion to one like a son of man and the holy ones.

flow.label: Ram, goat and seventy weeks
flow.detail: Persia and Greece clash; a little horn desecrates the sanctuary; Daniel's confession brings the seventy-weeks revelation.

flow.label: Kings of north and south
flow.detail: An angel recounts centuries of conflict ending with a blasphemous king and a time of distress.

flow.label: Resurrection and the end
flow.detail: Michael arises, the dead awake to life or shame, the wise shine like stars, and Daniel is told to rest until the end.

keyWords.meaning: Kingdom, kingship, reign; the book's central theme, used dozens of times for human empires and God's everlasting reign.
'A human being'. In contrast to the beasts, a human figure comes with the clouds, the way God himself travels in the Old Testament, and receives eternal dominion.
A secret or hidden plan revealed by God, a word borrowed from Persian. It appears in the Dead Sea Scrolls and lies behind Paul's 'mystery'.
Holy ones or saints. In Dan 7 it may mean faithful Israel, angels, or both, who receive the kingdom.
Those who have insight and teach many; they will suffer but will shine like stars.

connections.how: Daniel at Nebuchadnezzar's court mirrors Joseph at Pharaoh's: a young exile interprets a king's dream when the experts fail and is promoted.
Daniel reads Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years and prays for its fulfilment.
Both are stories of Jews in foreign courts facing deadly decrees, showing faithful life in the diaspora.
Jesus warns of 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel' and claims the son of man's coming with the clouds before the high priest.
Revelation draws heavily on Daniel: the son of man, beasts from the sea, time-times-and-half, and books opened in judgment.
Hebrews alludes to those who 'shut the mouths of lions' and 'quenched the power of fire' as heroes of faith.

jesusLens: 'Son of Man' was Jesus' favourite way of referring to himself, and at his trial he joined Dan 7:13 to Ps 110:1: 'you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven' (Mark 14:62), a claim the high priest heard as blasphemy. Jesus' proclamation of 'the kingdom of God' takes up Daniel's promise of a kingdom God would set up that would never be destroyed (Dan 2:44; Mark 1:15). Revelation pictures the risen Jesus with features of both the son of man and the Ancient of Days (Rev 1:13-14; Dan 7:9). Many Christians have read the seventy weeks (Dan 9:24-27) as pointing to the time of the Messiah's coming and death. Jewish interpreters read the son of man as the Messiah or as Israel, and the seventy weeks as ending in the second-temple period, but do not identify the Messiah with Jesus. Critical scholars often read the original son of man as the archangel Michael or as a symbol of faithful Israel vindicated.

misreadings.topic: The seventieth week as a future seven-year tribulation
misreadings.popular: Dan 9:27 predicts that a future Antichrist will make a seven-year peace treaty with Israel, break it halfway, and set up an abomination in a rebuilt temple; there is a long gap (the church age) between the 69th and 70th weeks.
misreadings.inContext: The 'gap' and future Antichrist reading developed mainly in 19th-century dispensationalism (J. N. Darby, later the Scofield Bible). Other readings are older and widely held: the seventy weeks end with Antiochus IV in 167-164 BC (most critical scholars, e.g. John Collins); or they culminate in the Messiah's death and the temple's destruction in AD 70 (many early church writers, Reformed and other evangelical scholars). The numbers are probably symbolic (ten jubilee cycles of seven times seven years). Scholars such as Ernest Lucas and Tremper Longman note how differently the details can be calculated.
misreadings.defence: Dispensational scholars such as John Walvoord, Harold Hoehner (who calculated the 69 weeks precisely to AD 33) and Stephen Miller defend the future-week view, arguing that the six goals of Dan 9:24 are not yet fully accomplished and that Jesus placed the 'abomination' in the future (Matt 24:15). This is a genuine debate among evangelicals, not simply a popular mistake.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Which reading one holds shapes views of Israel, the end times and current events. Knowing that faithful scholars disagree guards against treating one end-times chart as essential to the gospel.

misreadings.topic: Daniel 1 as a diet plan
misreadings.popular: Daniel's vegetables-and-water diet is a biblical model for healthy eating or a spiritual 'Daniel Fast' that guarantees health and breakthroughs.
misreadings.inContext: Daniel's concern was loyalty, not nutrition. Eating the king's food would mark him as the king's dependant and perhaps involve unclean or idol-offered food (Dan 1:8). The point of the ten-day test is that God, not the king's rich table, gave them health and wisdom (Dan 1:17). Later Daniel eats normally and fasts from meat and wine only during a period of mourning (Dan 10:2-3). Commentators across traditions (Goldingay, Longman, Lucas) agree.
misreadings.defence: Many evangelical teachers who promote the 'Daniel Fast' present it as a voluntary spiritual discipline inspired by the text, not as a command or guarantee, which is reasonable. The concern is only when it is taught as the meaning of Dan 1.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The real lesson is how to serve faithfully inside a powerful system without being owned by it, a question for every believer in work and public life.

relevance.then: Daniel taught Jews under pagan empires, from Babylon to Antiochus IV, that God still ruled, that faithfulness was worth dying for, and that God would vindicate the faithful, even beyond death.
relevance.now: Daniel helps believers serve faithfully in secular institutions, resist the pull of powers that demand ultimate loyalty, pray with confession and hope, and trust that all empires are temporary while God's kingdom endures.
